<meta>This page serves as the formal introduction to the Apocrypha section of a Dutch Bible from 1604. It establishes the theological boundary between the "Canonical" books (considered the divinely inspired Word of God) and the "Apocryphal" books (considered useful but human-authored).</meta>

# THE BOOKS
## NAMED¹ APOCRYPHA.

<margin>
1 **Apocrypha** is a Greek word signifying that which is secret and hidden. Therefore, the ancient Fathers <note>The "Church Fathers" were influential Christian theologians and scholars from the 1st to 8th centuries AD.</note> rightly assigned this name to these books because the teaching contained within is not accepted for the confirmation of faith, nor as authentic, but as private and personal writings. And although the ancient Fathers read them in the church—as St. Jerome recounts in the *Exposition of the Creed* by Rufinus <note>original: "int Symbolum van Ruffinus." Jerome (c. 347–420) was the translator of the Latin Vulgate Bible; Rufinus was a contemporary theologian.</note>—and though many things from them were written by the Apostles in the New Testament, nevertheless, because many places are found that openly conflict with the truth, they have at no time held authority, nor been approved to confirm doctrine in the same way as the other Canonical books, whose teaching was given through the Holy Spirit. See what St. Jerome has written about this in *Homily 1 on the Song of Songs*.
</margin>

### Warning to the Reader.

These books, which are called **Apocrypha**, have at all times been distinguished from the books that are considered without doubt to be **Holy Scripture**. For the ancient Fathers, wishing to ensure that no unholy books would be admitted alongside the books undoubtedly written by the Holy Spirit, created a roll which they called the **Canon**, that is, the **Rule**: thereby indicating that all the books contained therein were a certain Rule to which one must adhere. Regarding these books, they called them **Apocrypha**, thereby indicating that they should be regarded as private and personal writings, and not as authentic, like official sealed and approved documents. Therefore, there is such a distinction between these books and the others as there is between a letter that has been processed and sealed by a Notary—to be accepted by all people—and a letter written by a private individual.

It is true that they are not to be despised, as they contain good and useful teachings. However, it is nonetheless quite right that what has been given to us by the Holy Spirit should be esteemed and held above that which has come from men.

Revelation 14, verse 15" <note>original Latin: "MITTE FALCEM TUAM ET METE QUIA ARVIT MESSIS TERRE : APOCAL . 14 VERS . 15"</note>. The oval is framed by ornate architectural scrolls, two seated human figures at the top corners, and cherub-like faces at the sides and bottom.</image-desc>

# THE BOOKS
## CALLED <gloss>1</gloss> APOCRYPHA.

### A Warning to the Reader.

<margin>
1 <term>Apocrypha</term> is a Greek word <note>original: "Apocryphos"</note> signifying that which is secret and hidden. Therefore, the ancient Church Fathers rightly assigned this name to these books, because the teaching contained within them was never accepted for the confirmation of faith, nor as authentic, but rather as private and personal writings. And although the ancient Fathers read them in the churches—as <term>Saint Jerome</term> relates in the <term>Commentary on the Creed</term> by <term>Rufinus</term> <note>Jerome and Rufinus of Aquileia were 4th-century scholars who debated which books belonged in the Bible</note>, and although many things from them were quoted by the Apostles in the New Testament—nevertheless, because many passages are found that openly conflict with the truth, they have at no time held authority, nor been approved to confirm doctrine in the same way as the other Canonical books, whose teaching was given through the Holy Spirit. See what Saint Jerome has written regarding this in his first Homily on the <term>Song of Songs</term> <note>original: "Canticum Canticorum"</note>.
</margin>

THese Books which are called <term>Apocrypha</term> have at all times been distinguished from the Books which are considered without doubt to be of the Holy Scripture. For the ancient Fathers, wishing to ensure that no unholy Books would be permitted alongside the Books which were undoubtedly written by the Holy Spirit, made a roll which they called the **Canon**, that is, the **Rule**: thereby indicating that all the Books contained therein were a certain Rule, to which one must adhere. Regarding these Books, they called them *Apocrypha*, thereby indicating that they should be regarded as private and personal writings, and not as authentic, like public, sealed, and approved Letters. Therefore, there is such a distinction between these Books and the others, as between a Letter that has been formally processed and sealed by a Notary—to be accepted by all people—and a Letter written by a private individual.

It is true that they are not to be despised, as they contain good and useful teaching. But it is nevertheless quite right that what has been given to us through the Holy Spirit should be esteemed and held above that which has come from men.

# THE THIRD BOOK 
### OF ESDRAS.

### Brief summary of this Book.

->The third book of Esdras relates certain things from the fourth book of Kings, and also many things that are explained in the books of Ezra and Nehemiah, although some things are shown here more broadly, and many beautiful examples of godliness are set before our eyes.<-

---

<margin>
1 Otherwise: The first. It is called the third book of Esdras in view of the two other books that are approved by the church; namely, the first which is simply called Ezra, and the other called Nehemiah, gathered by the same Ezra: yet the order of history has moved some to call this book the first book of Esdras, because the content of this book occurred before that which is described in the other two books; however, it is not known for certain who the author of these books is: nevertheless, it is attributed to him because the Holy Spirit used him to gather and put into writing many things that serve for the instruction of his church: yet the correct use of this book and the others called Apocrypha shall be that we accept them as pure and true doctrine, insofar as they agree with other books of the Holy Scripture; therefore, they should be read with judgment and good discernment.
</margin>

</margin>

# Ezra <note>original: "Esdrae"</note>

<margin>4 There were many of the Priests and Levites whom the Lord did not move in spirit, and therefore they did not set out for the journey, as did Ezra and Nehemiah and their company.</margin>

# The Third Book

<margin>
5 This number is described in various ways; for in some books it speaks of those who have their descent from specific persons, and in others of those who came from certain cities in the land of Canaan. Furthermore, this number is very different from what is currently found in Holy Scripture in this manner <note>referring to discrepancies between this book and the lists in Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7</note>, and there are also some useless repetitions of certain names. This is partly the reason why this book is not accepted to confirm doubtful matters of doctrine. Nevertheless, the ancient Church fathers made no distinction between this book and others called **Apocryphi** <note>original: "Apocryphi"; books of the Bible not included in the Hebrew canon but used by the Church</note>, and they valued it more than those they completely rejected, such as the Book of Adam's Conversion, the Testament of Job, the battle between the giants and the dragon, and similar others written by the Jews. They openly called those rejected books "Apocryphal," while these were called "Ecclesiastical," and the others, whose truth is not doubted, "Canonical."

### The 8th Chapter.

1. Ezra, a scribe and well-versed in the Law of Moses, comes from Babylon to Jerusalem. 10. The contents of the letter which Artaxerxes gave to Ezra. 28. Ezra praises and thanks the Lord. 31. The number of those who traveled with Ezra from Babylon to Judea.

2. The son of Zadok, the son of Ahitub, the son of Amariah, the son of Bukki, the son of Abishua, the son of Phinehas, the son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron, the first Priest.

3. All these people had still remained in captivity.

4. From this it is evident that it was up to the people to either journey up to the land or to remain in captivity, just as it was in the time of King Cyrus; therefore, there were many who preferred to stay in captivity rather than journey to their land.
</margin>

11. I have recognized, out of friendship and goodwill, and commanded, that if perhaps anyone from the Jews, from the Priests and Levites, who are in my kingdom, has a desire and will to journey with you to Jerusalem, that he may do so.
12. And therefore, if some wish to journey with you, let them come together and travel with you, as it pleases me and my seven Counselors.
13. That they may see what is being done in Jerusalem and in Judea.
14. And maintain things as you find them in the Law of the Lord.
15. And bring gifts to God, the Lord of Israel, which I and my friends have promised to Jerusalem; also all the silver and gold that is in the land of Babylon, to the Lord in Jerusalem.
16. Along with that which is donated for the people in the Temple of the Lord in Jerusalem; yes, that this same silver and gold be collected, and additionally, rams for offering, sheep, and goats, and other things belonging to the same.

<column-break/>

17. And that they should offer to the Lord upon the Altar of their Lord, which is in Jerusalem.
18. And everything that you and your brothers wish to do with the silver and gold, do that according to your will, and according to the commandment of your God.
19. Also with all the holy vessels which are given to you for the service of the house of the Lord your God in Jerusalem.
20. And whatever else is necessary for you for the work of the Temple, that shall be given to you from the royal treasury; and what you, along with your brothers, wish to do with the gold and silver, do that according to the will of the Lord.
21. And I, King Artaxerxes, have commanded the keepers of the treasures in Syria and Phoenicia <note>original: "Syria en Phenice"</note> that they should provide everything that Ezra the Priest, instructed in the Law of the Lord, shall write.

<margin>
5. This is a jar with two handles <note>term: "back met twee ooren" - a traditional description of a storage vessel</note> of a certain measure, and in Ezra 7:21 (where this matter is handled) it is a hundred bath of wine: what "cor" and "bath" mean, and how much they hold, see 1 Kings 11.
</margin>

22. Silver, up to a hundred hundredweights <note>original: "centeners"</note>, likewise also of gold, grain, up to a hundred bushels <note>original: "mudde"</note>; wine, up to a hundred barrels <note>original: "amen"</note>; and other things which one has in abundance without number.
23. Everything shall be done for the most high God according to His Law, so that the wrath of God does not arise against the kingdom of the King and his children.
24. Furthermore, I command you that upon the Priests, Levites, Singers, and also the ministers of the Temple, as well as the scribes,
25. You shall lay no tribute or tax, and no one shall have the power to act against them.
26. You, however, Ezra, according to your wisdom, appoint Judges and magistrates throughout all Syria and Phoenicia, and teach all those who do not know the Law of the Lord your God.

<margin>
6. Since the principal part of the judicial office consists in ensuring that God is given what is due to Him, and since no one can do this who is not instructed in the Law, it is therefore necessary with great zeal that the Rulers of the land, and those to whom the care of justice is commanded, be gifted with the knowledge of the Law.
</margin>

27. And all those who transgress the Law, let them be punished, whether with death, or otherwise with physical punishment, or with a monetary fine, or with banishment.
28. Then Ezra the scribe said: Praised be the God of our fathers, who has put such a will into the heart of the King to make glorious His house which is in Jerusalem.
29. And who has made me acceptable before the King, before his counselors, his friends, and nobles.

<margin>
7. That is: I, Ezra. Previously he spoke of himself in the third person.
</margin>

30. And I became steadfast in my spirit as God my Lord helped me, and I chose men from Israel who went up with me in groups.

<margin>
8. Note: The seventh year of Darius Longimanus, also named Artaxerxes. See the map for Ezra, 1 Ezra 8:1, where this matter is handled.
</margin>

31. And these are the heads, according to their generations and their fathers' houses, who went up with me from Babylon out of the kingdom of Artaxerxes.
32. From the children of Perez: Gershom. From the children of Shemaiah: Amenus. From the children of David: Hattush, the son of Shechaniah.
33. From the children of Parosh: Zechariah; and with him returned one hundred and fifty men.

<margin>
9. Others say Gamael: but here he is well named; likewise it is also with the other names, from which one can observe that the ancients had various names, which is the cause of the disputes found in Scripture between names, to which one should nonetheless not pay great heed. See the note here on 1 Chronicles 3:5.
</margin>

37. From the children of Elam: Jeshaiah son of Athaliah, and with him eighty.
38. From the children of Shephatiah: Zebadiah son of Michael, and with him two hundred and twelve men.
39. From the children of Bani: Shelomith the son of Josiphiah, and with him one hundred and sixty men.

# THE FOURTH BOOK
## EZRA.

->Brief contents of this book.<-

The fourth book of Ezra contains visions and revelations, encompassing various histories of the people. The ancients regarded this book the least among those mentioned above; nevertheless, they did not entirely reject it, for it has its usefulness. <note>4 Ezra was often excluded from the formal canon but remained popular for its apocalyptic imagery.</note>

### The First Chapter.

<margin>
**Chap. 1.**
1 This book is named the second and fourth book, for the same reason that the preceding was named the first and third, regarding which one may see the notes on the previous book: however, the right use of this one (as with the other Apocrypha) lies in this: that one shall take from it for instruction that which accords with the other books of scripture, which are without doubt written by the Holy Spirit; and if anything is found in it that does not agree, one shall hold it as suspect; wherefore in the reading of it, a righteous judgment is necessary.
</margin>

<margin>
1 Ezra the Prophet. 4 Ezra holds before the Jews their ungratefulness. 37 The Gentiles shall not see with physical eyes, but shall believe with the heart. 39 Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Hosea, Amos, Micah, Joel, Obadiah, Jonah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi, the faithful of the Gentiles.
</margin>

<summary>This page introduces the Fourth Book of Ezra (2 Esdras), where God enumerates the many miracles performed for Israel during the Exodus and contrasts them with the people's persistent ungratefulness and idolatry. The text culminates in a prophecy that God will reject Israel in favor of other nations who will honor His name.</summary>

<margin>
i Ezra is dejected, seeing the prosperity of the Babylonians and the oppression of the people of God.

1 IN the thirtieth year after the fall of the city, I was in Babylon, and lay troubled upon my bed, and many thoughts came into my heart.
2 For I saw the desolation of Zion and the abundance of those who dwelt in Babylon.
3 And my spirit was vehemently moved, so that I began to speak humble words to the Most High, and said:
4 O Sovereign Lord, you spoke from the beginning when you planted the earth (and that alone) and commanded the people:

### Ezra

<margin>6 As if he were saying: I do not investigate things that are heavenly, nor things involving the angels; but I wonder at such an unequal condition, namely that here below on earth the godless live in happiness and the good in sorrow, and how this all happens through the Lord’s will.</margin>
...speak of [heavenly] things, but of those which we handle daily; namely, why is Israel despised by the heathens? And why is the people, whom you have loved from all time, given over to be punished by godless nations? And why has the law of our fathers come to nothing, and the written covenant is nowhere to be found?

24 And we have passed away from the world like locusts, and our life is a fear, and we are not worthy to obtain mercy.

<margin>7 He means to say that he is greatly troubled by this: that the unbelievers blaspheme the name of the Lord and mock his servants in the midst of oppression, saying: Where is their God? etc. Yet this is not lamented here.</margin>
25 What will he then do <insert>for his name,</insert> which is called upon over us? Of these things have I asked.

26 Then he answered me and said: The more you search, the more you shall wonder, for the time runs away in haste.

27 And you cannot understand what is promised to the righteous in future times: for this time is full of wickedness and weakness.

<margin>8 Man has a set time here on earth, and cannot see what end his affairs shall have; and therefore, matters cannot be rightly judged here.</margin>
28 But regarding what you ask me, I will tell you: evil is sown, but its destruction is not yet here.

29 If now the evil that is sown is not overturned, and the place where that evil is sown does not pass away, then that which is sown with good cannot come.

<margin>9 This agrees in spirit with the parable of the weeds in Matthew 13, in which we are taught that the course of this world is laid out in great confusion without any distinction, and that many things remain covered and hidden until the time of the gathering into the barn.</margin>
30 For the seed of evil was sown in the heart of man by the evil one from the beginning: how much godlessness has it brought forth until this time? And how much shall it yet bring forth, until one comes to the threshing floor?

31 Now measure for yourself what a great fruit of godlessness the evil seed has brought forth?

<margin>10 It is impossible for any good to come forth from our nature, so long as it is not changed or renewed. Genesis 3.</margin>
32 And if its ears of grain, which are without number, are cut down, what a great barn shall they fill?

<margin>11 This answer refers to the preceding verse, "when comes the fruit," etc.</margin>
33 Then I said: How so, and when shall that be? Why are our years so few and so miserable?

34 Then he answered and said to me: Do not hasten too much above the Most High; for your hastening to be above him is in vain, you demand too much of him.

35 Have not the souls of the pious, even in their heavenly dwelling, asked about these things, saying: How long shall I hope thus? When comes the fruit of my barn, and of my reward?

<margin>12 God has ordained certain hours and times for that which shall be, and it does not belong to man to know or even to divide the times which the Lord has placed in his own power. Acts 1:7.</margin>

37 And in <insert>measure,</insert> he has measured the time, and by number he has numbered the time, and he does not move nor stir it until the same measure is fulfilled.

38 Then I answered and said: O Lord Ruler, now we are all full of sins.

39 May it not be for our sake that the barn of the righteous is not filled, because of the sins of those who dwell on earth.

<margin>13 He demonstrates by this example that the time ordained for the gathering of the good, which is the last day, shall not be hastened nor delayed by any human means, be it good or evil or the like.</margin>

<vocab>
**Ezra**: (Esdra) The prophet and protagonist of the book.
**Merciful**: (barmhertich) Showing compassion or forgiveness.
**Womb**: (baermoeder) Literally "mother of the belly," referring to the place of gestation.
**Angels**: (Enghelen) Divine messengers of God.
**Gentiles**: (Heydenen) Literally "Heathens," referring to non-Jewish nations.
**Prophets**: (Propheten) Divinely inspired teachers or revealers of God's will.
**Righteousness**: (gerechticheyt) Morally right or justifiable behavior.
**Creatures**: (schepsels) Created beings.
</vocab>

<summary>Ezra pleads with God for mercy, arguing that since God took such great care to form human life in the womb, He should be equally diligent in preserving it from destruction. The text introduces Ezra's famous prayer, contrasting human frailty and sin with God's eternal majesty and the few who will be saved.</summary>
<keywords>Ezra, mercy, creation, womb, salvation of the few, angels, divine judgment, Israel, righteousness, original sin</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the visionary experiences of the prophet Ezra (Esdras) as recorded in the apocryphal Fourth Book of Ezra. Following his previous visions regarding the state of Israel and the soul, Ezra now receives a grand political and prophetic vision concerning the rise and fall of empires, symbolized by an eagle and a lion.</meta>

The Fourth Book

I remained there that same night and the next, just as he had commanded me.

### The 11th Chapter.

1. Ezra sees an eagle flying up from the sea. 37. And a lion running as if out of the woods. 42. God punishes the excess and vileness of the powerful.

<margin>Chapter 11.
a Daniel 7:1.
b Ezekiel 1:10, 10:14, 17:3.
Daniel 7:4.</margin>
<margin>1 The meaning of this vision is explained in the following chapter, verse 11. Daniel 7 (in the vision of the four beasts) signifies the four Monarchies, the beginnings of which came up from the Sea; likewise, the Eagle is mentioned here to represent the greatness of the matter, along with its twelve wings and three heads, as seen in the following chapter, verse 14.</margin>
<margin>2 Daniel chapter 7 mentions the four winds of heaven that stormed against each other on the Great Sea, representing the upheavals at the beginning of the four Monarchies; but since the following chapter, verse 11, says that this vision regarding a king corresponds with what Daniel saw, this vision must be understood with the same meaning.</margin>
<margin>3 Beyond what is said in the explanation of this vision in the following chapter, it will be useful to understand what happened during the Monarchy of the Greeks until the coming of Christ. Regarding this, one should first note that there were eight Kings: the first was Alexander the Great, who reigned only twelve years; Seleucus Nicanor, thirty-two years; Antiochus Soter, thirty-three years; Antiochus Theos, fifteen years; Seleucus Callinicus, twenty years; Seleucus Ceraunus, three years; Antiochus the Great, thirty-six years; Seleucus Philopator, twelve years. After him came Antiochus Epiphanes, the tyrant. From the time of Judas Maccabeus, who was also a Prince of the Jews, there were also eight successors in the kingdom, one after the other, until the time of Herod, who obtained dominion over the Jews; Christ was born in the thirty-second year of his reign.</margin>
<margin>4 This, along with what follows, is explained in the text of the next chapter.</margin>
1 **A**nd I saw a dream, and behold, an eagle flew up from the sea, which had twelve wings and three heads.
2 And as I looked, it stretched its wings over all the earth, and all the winds blew upon them, and they were gathered together again.
3 And I saw that from its feathers, other small feathers grew.
4 The heads were at rest: the middle head was larger than the others, yet it also rested with them.
5 Furthermore, I saw that the eagle flew with its wings and ruled over the earth, and over all who dwell upon the earth.
6 Everything under heaven was subject to it: no one resisted it, not even a single creature on the face of the earth.
7 Furthermore, I saw how the eagle stood up on its claws and spoke with its wings, saying:
8 You shall not all watch together; let each one sleep in his own place, and watch by turns.
9 The heads, however, were preserved for the end.
10 And I saw that the voice did not come from its heads, but from the middle of its body.
11 I counted the other feathers that were opposite them; there were eight.
12 And I looked, and behold, a feather rose up on the right side and ruled over all the earth.
13 And it happened that while it ruled, its end came, and its place appeared no more; then the next one rose up and ruled, and it had a long time.
14 And while it ruled, its end also came, like the previous one, so that it appeared nowhere anymore.
15 Then a voice came to it and said:
16 Listen, you who have held the world for so long: this I say to you, before you cease to be.
17 No one after your time shall hold it, not even for half the time.
18 Then the third raised itself up and ruled like the previous ones, and it was also no more.
19 So it went with all the others, one after another, so that each ruled and then was no more.
20 Then I looked, and behold, in time the following feathers were raised up on the right side so that they also ruled; and some of those ruled, but in a short time they were seen no more.
21 For some of them were raised up, yet they did not rule.
22 After this I looked, and behold, the twelve wings were no longer there, nor the two small wings.
23 And there was nothing left on the body of the eagle but two heads that rested, and six small feathers.
24 Yet I looked further, and saw that the six small feathers were divided into two, and remained under the head that was on the right side; for four remained in their place.

<column-break/>

25 Then I saw that those under the wings attempted to raise themselves up and to rule.
26 Then one was raised up, but in a short time it was nowhere to be seen.
27 And the others passed away even more quickly than the first.
28 Then the two that were still left also thought within themselves to rule.
29 And while they were thinking that, one of the resting heads awoke, namely, the largest and middle one.
30 And then I saw that two heads were joined with it.
31 And that head turned itself, with those that were with it, and swallowed the two lower wings that wanted to rule.
32 That head now terrified the whole world, and ruled on earth over those who lived on earth with much labor, and had power over the face of the earth, over all the wings that had been there.
33 After this I saw that the middle head suddenly was there no more, just as the wings had been.
34 Then the two heads remained, which also ruled over the earth, and over those who dwelt on the earth.
35 Then I saw how the head on the right side swallowed the one on the left.
<margin>5 Just as the wings that agreed with one another represent the division of one Kingdom against another; so too does the confusion of the heads.</margin>
36 And I heard a voice that spoke to me: Look before you, and consider what you see.
37 And I looked, and behold, a lion roared there, running quickly out of the woods, and sent out a human voice to the eagle, and spoke:
<margin>c 2 Esdras 12:31.</margin>
38 Listen, I will speak to you, and the Most High shall tell you:
39 Are you not the one that remains of the four beasts <note>original: "vier gesierten," referring to the four creatures in Daniel's vision</note> that I made to rule in my world, so that through them the end of their times might come?
40 And the fourth came, and overcame all the beasts that were past, and had power over the world with great terror, and over the whole earth with shameful labor, and dwelt so long upon the earth with deceit.
<margin>d Daniel 7:7.</margin>
41 And you did not judge the earth with truth.
42 For you afflict the meek, you hinder the quiet; you loved liars, and destroyed the dwellings of those who brought forth fruit, and threw down the walls of those who did you no harm.
43 Therefore, your injustice has reached the Most High, and your pride has reached the Mighty One.
44 And the Most High has looked upon the proud times: and behold, they are ended, and their blasphemies are fulfilled.
45 And therefore, you eagle, appear no more, nor your horrible wings, nor your evil feathers, nor your malicious heads, nor your shameful claws, nor all your idle body.
46 So that the earth may be refreshed again, being delivered from your violence, and that she may hope for the judgment and mercy of Him who made her.

Marginal notes link this imagery to the four monarchies of Daniel and historical Greek rulers like Alexander the Great and the Seleucid dynasty.</summary>

# Ezra.

<margin>1 This Eagle is destroyed and brought to nothing by the hand of the Romans under verse 32. Previously, the continuation of the three Monarchies was depicted there. <note>original: "a Dan. 7.1"</note></margin>

And from the time of King Nebuchadnezzar (who established the kingdom) until Darius, who was the last in the Monarchy of the Persians, one finds that there were twelve: see the map before the book of Ezra. ### Chapter 13.

->1. Esdras <note>Ezra</note> sees a wind rise from the sea, which wind becomes a man. 5. People fight against him who came up from the sea. 10. He pierces through them with the wind of his mouth. 13. Many people come to him in sorrow, etc. 25. The interpretation of the man climbing up from the sea. 32. The Son of God shall be revealed. 36. <margin>
Chapter 13.
1 By the wind is understood a great disturbance that shall be in the world (signified by the Sea): the waters are the rebellious people who rise up against one another.
2 This must be interpreted as referring to Christ, and is explained as such under verse 16. Likewise, what follows in the very next verse proves to us with how much great honor and majesty he shall appear a second time.
3 The entire world has set itself against Christ; the Jews mocked him, the Heathen spat upon him, and even today he is persecuted and must suffer oppression in his members <note>the "members" refers to the body of believers</note> and the rejection of the world.
4 He means to say, whatever struggle the world takes up against Christ, he shall always remain a conqueror. Therefore, by the mountain (spoken of here) is understood faith, righteousness, and holiness, which are like a high wall where the enemies can gain no access to cause harm.
5 Those who set themselves against Christ are in constant misery and burdened with terror in their conscience.
a Isaiah 66:16, Ephesians 6:17, Revelation 1:16 / 19:15.
6 See here how Christ the Lord destroys his enemies, not by sword or any fleshly power, but by the breath of his mouth: that is, by his divine word, which is signified here by fire, because of the power and life-giving force within it, which no power can withstand.
7 These are the elect of the Lord, of whom some are joyful, namely those who feel within themselves the peace of conscience and the fatherly love of Christ; others are sad, who, being burdened with the weight of sin, come to Christ with sincere repentance; others are bound, who are brought to him by force.
</margin>

1 AFTER seven days it happened that I dreamed a dream by night:

2 There arose a wind from the sea, so that it moved all the waves <note>original: "bloeden," an archaic term for billows/floods</note> of the sea.

3 And I saw that this man became strong and took flight with the clouds of heaven; and whenever he turned his face to look, everything that was seen beneath him trembled.

4 And whenever a voice went out of his mouth, all who heard him burned, as the earth melts when it feels the fire.

5 After this I saw that many people gathered together, so many that no one could count them, coming from the four winds of heaven to fight the man who rose from the sea.

6 And behold, he had carved out for himself a high mountain and flew upon it.

7 But I wished to see the region or the place where the mountain was carved out, but I could not.

8 After this I saw that all those who had come together to fight him were exceedingly afraid, yet they dared to fight.

9 When I now saw the assault of the people, he lifted neither hand nor blade, nor indeed any weapon at all:

10 But he sent out of his mouth only a blast as of fire, and from his lips a flame, and from his tongue sparks and tempests.

11 And all were mixed together—the fire, the flame, and the tempest—and fell upon the multitude that had prepared to fight him with violence, and burned them all, so that of the entire multitude finally nothing more was seen than dust and smoke: when I saw this, I was afraid.

12 After this I saw the same man come down from the mountain and call to himself another peaceful multitude.

13 And many people came to him; some were joyful, some were sad, some among them were bound, and they were led and brought forward. Then I became weak from great terror, and I awoke and said:

<column-break/>

14 You have shown your servant all these wonders from the beginning, and have accounted me worthy that you should receive my prayer.

15 So show me now the interpretation of this dream.

16 For thus I consider in my understanding: woe to those who are left in those days, and much more woe to those who are not left.

17 For those who were not left were sorrowful.

<margin>
8 There was a question of two kinds of "left" ones <note>survivors</note>: the first for destruction, which for a certain time they could not escape; the others were left for oppression, and that only for a certain time; and of this second kind he speaks in the following verse.
</margin>

18 I understand now the things that are reserved for the last days, and what shall happen to them: also to those who are not left.

19 Therefore they have come into great danger and much necessity, as these dreams show.

<meta>This page continues the translation of 2 Esdras (also known as 4 Ezra). On the previous page, Ezra was being given a vision of the end times. Here, in Chapter 14, God commands Ezra to gather five scribes and prepare to restore the Holy Scriptures, which had been lost or burned during the destruction of Jerusalem. Chapter 15 begins a series of prophecies regarding God's judgment on the nations, particularly "Egypt" (often interpreted here as a symbolic name for Babylon or oppressive worldly powers).</meta>

# THE BOOK
## TOBIT.
->Short summary of this Book.<-

Tobit was a godly man, filled with the love of God and his neighbor, of the tribe of Naphtali, from a chief city of the same tribe, bearing the name of the tribe, situated in Upper Galilee near the Jordan: this holy man was also carried away captive by King Shalmaneser into Assyria, in the ninth year of Hoshea the King of Israel, which captivity is recounted in 2 Kings 17. And while he was in that same captivity, he conducted himself so godlily, that he was a mirror of virtue and holiness both to his own people and to the Heathen: his glorious deeds and works are recounted in this book, which is therefore titled with his name, just as many other fine worldly books bear the names of the persons whose works and honorable facts are described therein: it is uncertain who the author hereof is, yet because of the teaching contained therein, which greatly serves for instruction unto godliness, the ancient fathers have deemed this same book or history worthy to be accepted into the number, not of the Canonical books, but of those which may bring great usefulness to the church; yet one must read this same on the way and manner as has been said of the other Apocrypha, at the beginning of the third book of Esdras.

# T H E B O O K
# J U D I T H.

### Brief content of this Book.

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap N with floral and leaf patterns.</image-desc>
After the children of Israel had come out of captivity into their land, and Jerusalem was established, and the temple was made fit for the service of the Lord, they settled themselves in various places and cities, where they lived in stillness and peace. But the Lord, knowing well that man, by the nature of his corrupt essence, is very inclined (especially in times of peace) to live according to the flesh and to forget the Lord, exercised oppression and anxieties to deliver his people therefrom. He kept such a mighty army in their land that the earth trembled from it; this army was led by Nebuchadnezzar, the cause of which is described in the explanation of the fifth verse of the first chapter. His governor and field commander was Holofernes, who intended to subdue all places he passed with force, so that they would acknowledge Nebuchadnezzar his master as the only God. And while he came into the Jewish land with such great power and violence, the Jews were so distressed and dismayed that they could perceive nothing on all sides but a destruction and devastation of the entire land. Which the Lord allowed to happen, so that his glory would be made more manifest, and that everyone would acknowledge that he alone could assist his people in their utmost need. Which he also finally did, not through any valiant Captain, but through his handmaid Judith, a humble woman, through whom he put the proud Tyrant and his entire army to shame; for she cut off his head and drove his soldiers to flight, who left behind all their goods and baggage to save themselves. Thus the Lord always uses that which is infirm and weak to accomplish his wonderful works, for which we must praise his goodness, as he always has a regard for his children. This book is entitled with the name Judith because her virtue <note>or "bravery," original: "vromicheyt"</note>, which she received from the Lord for the deliverance of the people, is described therein. The author of this book is uncertain; nevertheless, the church has always allowed it to be read for the utility and teaching contained within it.

### The 11th Chapter.

->1. Holofernes encourages Judith to have good courage; 3. he asks her the reason for her coming; 4. Judith deceives Holofernes with beautiful words.<-

<margin>1 <gloss>Some who try to excuse the noble Judith from hypocrisy through a sharp interpretation say that she outwardly related a matter, while beneath her words was another mystery; but the text must be understood simply, following the interpretation of the previous Chapter, verse 13.</gloss></margin>
AND Holofernes said to her: Have good courage, and do not fear: for I have never harmed a person who has surrendered himself to King Nebuchadnezzar.
2 And if your people had not despised me, I would never have raised a spear against them.
3 Now tell me here, why you have fled from them and come to me.
<margin>2 <gloss>Otherwise: I promise you by the life of King Nebuchadnezzar, etc. Just as Joseph, speaking to his brothers and swearing by the life of King Pharaoh, sinned (Gen. 42:15), so this godly woman cannot be innocent, since she continues in falsehood after speaking with deceit; she then swears by the life of a godless King, from which one may understand that even the holiest here in the world often fall greatly.</gloss></margin>
4 Judith answered and said: If you would graciously hear your handmaid, and if you do as your handmaid shall tell you, then the Lord will give you success and victory.
5 May God give Nebuchadnezzar success and prosperity, the King of all the land, who has sent you to punish all the disobedient: for you can make not only the people but also all the animals in the land subject to him.
6 For your ingenuity and wisdom are praised in the whole world, and everyone knows that you are the most powerful prince in the whole Kingdom, and your good government is praised everywhere.
7 <margin>a Judith 5:5.</margin> So we also know what Achior has spoken, and how you have acted against him for it.
8 For our God is so angry over our sins that He has caused it to be proclaimed through His Prophets: He will punish the people because of their sins.
9 Since the people of Israel now know that they have angered their God, they are terrified of you.
10 Moreover, they suffer great hunger and must perish from thirst.
<margin>3 <gloss>Otherwise: And all the more because what is forbidden by God is, etc. Just as David and those with him were forced by the law of necessity to eat the showbread against the command of the Law (Matt. 12:3), so this people, without committing a sin in their great need, could have eaten the food that was forbidden to them in the Law of God.</gloss></margin>
11 And they have now purposed to slaughter their cattle so that they may drink their blood.
12 And to eat the holy offerings—of corn, wine, and oil—which God has forbidden them, so that they should not even touch them: Therefore it is certain that they must perish, since they do such things.
13 <margin>b Judith 10:12.</margin> And since I know that, I have fled from them, and the Lord has sent me to you to tell you such things.
14 For although I have come to you, I have not fallen away from God because of it, but I wish still to serve my God with you: and your handmaid shall go out and pray to God.
<margin>4 <gloss>Otherwise: God has sent me to you to deal with this, of which the whole earth shall be amazed, etc. This was fulfilled when she cut off Holofernes' head. She gives this reason so that she might obtain freedom to go out into the valley outside the camp, under the pretense of praying to her God, which she could not have done in the camp without being defiled. And having obtained this freedom, she could carry out her plan with greater boldness.</gloss></margin>
15 He shall reveal to me when He will give them their reward for their sin, so I will then come and tell you, and lead you through the middle of Jerusalem, so that you shall have all that people of Israel like sheep that have no shepherd: and not one dog shall dare to bark at you.

<margin>Cap. xj.</margin>

<meta>This page concludes the narrative of the Book of Judith. # The Book of Judith.

<margin>$\ast$ Note: To confirm the blessings of the Lord, etc. That is: To praise and thank the Lord for all the rich blessings he had shown to his people, just as Melchizedek did, who came to meet Abraham when he had gained victory over the four kings, Genesis 14:24.</margin>

<margin>$\dagger$ All these honorable titles must be attributed to God alone; therefore it was not rightly done by the High Priest and the entire people to honor this woman with them. Also, the High Priest should have remained within Jerusalem to offer sacrifices to the Lord with the other people according to the order of the law, and to praise and thank him for the blessing he had shown in Israel, just as happened in the time of Hezekiah, Josiah, and other godly kings. Therefore, this should not be an example for us to follow. <note>This marginal note reflects a Reformation-era critique, cautioning readers not to praise humans (Judith) where praise belongs to God, and criticizing the High Priest for leaving his post at the Temple.</note></margin>

9 After that, Jehoiakim the High Priest came from Jerusalem to Bethulia with all the priests, so that they might see Judith.
10 And she went out to meet them: Then they all praised her together and spoke: You are the crown of Jerusalem, you are the joy of Israel’s heart, you are an honor to the entire people.
11 Because you have done such a praiseworthy deed and shown Israel such great kindness, so that God has helped them again: blessed are you before God eternally.

# WISDOM, THE
## BOOK OF
### WISDOM.

->Brief summary of this Book.<-

In the first book of Kings, in the 4th chapter, verse 32, it is written that Solomon spoke three thousand proverbs or notable sayings, and that his songs numbered one thousand and five, which number is not found in the books certainly written through the inspiration of the Spirit; but as it is well to think that among so many Godly men who daily conversed in the King’s court (to hear his wisdom, which was spread throughout the entire world) there were some who gathered these same proverbs, as much for their own instruction as for their descendants, collecting them together like a pile of precious pearls, without maintaining any order in the sequence of the subject matter. Which collection of proverbs is named the Book of Wisdom, because therein is treated the origin and fountain of wisdom, its dignity, its fruit, how necessary it is to all people, and its various workings. Regarding the Author, nothing certain is found, other than that the Church Fathers have thought it to have been Philo, a Jew: basing their opinion on the fact that this book was found only in the Greek language, in which language the same Philo wrote. And whatever the case may be, this has always been read in the church because of the beautiful teaching contained within it.

Fol. 119.
# WISDOM, THE BOOK OF WISDOM.
<note>original: "SAPIENTIA, HET BOECK DER WIISHEYT."</note>
<meta>catchword: him</meta>

### Short Summary of this Book.

In the first book of Kings, in the 4th chapter, verse 32, it is written that Solomon spoke three thousand proverbs or notable sayings, and that his songs numbered one thousand and five. This specific number is not found in the books certainly written by the inspiration of the Spirit. However, it is quite conceivable that among the many godly men who daily frequented the King's court—to hear his wisdom, which was renowned throughout the entire world—some gathered these same proverbs for their own instruction. They collected them for their descendants like a heap of precious pearls, without maintaining any strict order in the progression of the subject matter. This collection of proverbs is called the Book of Wisdom because it deals with the origin and fountain of wisdom, its worth, its fruit, how necessary it is for all people, and its various workings. Regarding the Author, nothing certain is found, other than that the Church Fathers believed it was Philo, a Jew. They based this opinion on the fact that this book was found only in the Greek language, in which Philo wrote. Whatever the case may be, it has always been read in the churches because of the beautiful teaching contained within it.

### The First Chapter.

1. Exhortation to the Rulers of the earth to seek the Lord. 4. The wicked heart is not worthy of wisdom. 5. The Holy Spirit flees the idolatrous and reckless. 6. God is a knower of the heart. 7. The spirit of the Lord fills the earth. 9. The plans and words of the godless must come before the judgment so that they may be punished. 11. Harmful slander and cursing. 13. God did not make death. 15. Righteousness is immortal.

<margin>
Chap. 1.
a Isaiah 65:1. Wisdom 5:1.
1 The Greek reads: "You who judge upon the earth." The word "judge" is used by the Hebrews to mean "to rule." This is modeled on the argument in the Book of Judges. Righteousness has two parts: the first concerns God, and the other concerns our neighbor. He begins with the first, concerning God.
b Deuteronomy 4:29. 2 Chronicles 15:4.
2 That is: By those who keep themselves from sins. For those who give themselves over to sin, well-knowing that it displeases God, tempt God because they do not fear His judgment.
3 Unbelief and mistrust pull us away from the knowledge of God.
4 The perverse opinions and approvals we have regarding God separate us from Him; this includes all idolaters, <term>Epicureans</term> <note>Followers of the philosopher Epicurus, often characterized in this period as those who live only for pleasure and deny the afterlife or divine providence.</note>, and apostates.
c Sirach 15:12.
5 Namely: Over those who tempt God.
d Jeremiah 4:18, 22.
6 By "wisdom" he understands the right and true knowledge of God.
7 The person who is not reborn through the spirit of God is here called "a body subject to sin," for where the spirit of the Lord does not rule, there is no wisdom.
8 That is: Who inspires science and teaching.
e John 14:26. 1 John 2:27.
9 The "reckless" are those who have not attained wisdom, as spoken of previously in the fourth book.
f Galatians 2:22.
g Jeremiah 17:2.
h Isaiah 6:3. Jeremiah 23:24. Acts 7:49. 1 Kings 2:44.
11 That is: His reasons and thoughts.
k Matthew 6:4. Hebrews 4:13.
</margin>

1 **L**ove righteousness, you Rulers of the earth; think that the Lord can help, and fear Him.
2 ^b For He lets Himself be found by those who ^2 do not tempt Him, and appears to those who do not ^3 mistrust Him.
3 But ^4 reckless opinions are far from God; and when punishment comes, it proves how foolish those people were.
4 For ^c wisdom does not enter into a wicked soul, and does not dwell in a body ^7 subject to sin.
5 ^d For the Holy Spirit, ^8 who teaches rightly, flees the idolatrous and withdraws from the ^9 reckless, who are punished by the sin that is poured out over them.
6 For ^f wisdom is so pious that she does not leave the slanderer unpunished: for God is a witness over all thoughts, and knows the feelings of all hearts, and hears all words.

1 SO hear now, you Kings, and understand; learn, you Judges of the ends of the earth.
2 Give ear, you who rule over many, you who <insert>2</insert> exalt yourselves over the nations.

8 For He, who is Lord over all, shall fear no person, nor stand in awe of any greatness; <margin>c</margin> He has made both the small and the great and cares <margin>4</margin> for all alike.
9 Now, a severe trial shall be held over the mighty.
10 To you, then, I speak, so that you may learn wisdom and not fail.
11 For whoever keeps holy things holily shall be held holy; and whoever learns them well shall find a defense.
12 Therefore, let my words please you; desire them and let yourselves be taught.
<margin>4 It is certain that God has a different care for His chosen children than for the godless and unbelieving, for He cares for His faithful with His grace and the gifts of the Spirit, which He does not give to the godless. Therefore, when it is said here that He carries equal care for all, it must be understood in this way: that just as He is the creator of all men, so He provides through His providence for every man that which is necessary for the maintenance of this life; for He lets His sun shine over the good and the evil, and lets His rain fall both over the righteous and the unrighteous. And that this is the correct sense may be understood from the words: He has made both the small and the great, etc.
5 The greater the office of our government that we receive from the Lord, the greater shall be the account that God will demand of our actions.
6 That is: He shall know how to answer for himself.

**12** For who will say to You: "What are You doing?" or who will withstand Your judgment? Or who will accuse You for the destruction of the heathens whom You have created? Or who will set himself against You as an avenger for the sake of unrighteous people?

**13** For there is no God besides You alone, You who care for all: so that You may prove how You do not judge unrighteously.

**14** For neither King nor tyrant can step before Your eyes to oppose You for those whom You punish.

**15** Since You are then righteous, You rule all things rightly, and You do not deem it fitting for Your majesty to condemn someone who has not deserved punishment.

**16** For Your strength is the dominion of righteousness: and since You rule over all, You also spare everyone.

**17** For You have proven Your strength to those who did not believe that You were so completely powerful.

**18** And You have shown Yourself to those who were arrogant; yet You, mighty Ruler, judge with gentleness and govern us with much forbearance: for You are able to do all that You will.

**19** Thus You teach Your people through such works that one must be pious and kind: and You give Your children to understand thereby that they shall be of good hope, for You are willing to accept repentance for sin.

**20** For if You punished the enemies of Your children, who were guilty of death, with such restraint and forbearance, and gave them time and space so that they could turn away from their wickedness.

**21** With how much greater consideration do You judge Your children, with whose fathers You established an oath and covenant of many good promises?

**22** Therefore, as often as You plague our enemies, You do so as a discipline for us, so that we may take heed of Your goodness with diligence; or if we are judged, that we shall nevertheless trust again in Your mercy.

**23** Therefore You also tormented the unrighteous, who led a foolish life, with their own abominations.

**24** For they had wandered so very far into error that they even held as gods the animals that were despised by their enemies, being deceived like foolish children.

**25** Therefore You also sent a mocking punishment among them, as among foolish children.

**26** Since such mocking warnings did not work, they experienced the earnest punishment of God.

**27** For they were tormented by the very things they held to be gods: which grieved them greatly when they saw them; those whom they previously refused to know, they now had to acknowledge as God: therefore also condemnation came upon them at the last.

### The 13th Chapter.

1. All people are by nature vain, nor have they recognized God through His works. 2. They have misused the works of God for idolatry. 3. The craftsman ought to be known through his works. 10. The idol-worshippers are unhappy. 11. The great ignorance and bluntness of the idol-worshippers.

<column-break/>

<margin>
1 Although the glory of God reveals itself in all creatures, nevertheless man is by nature so blinded that, seeing it, he cannot come to the fundamental knowledge [of God], but becomes confused in his thoughts.
a Romans 1:19.
</margin>
**All** people are truly naturally vain who know nothing of God, and do not recognize Him Who Is by visible goods: and do not see from the works who the Master is:

<margin>
b Deuteronomy 4:19, 17:3.
2 Some held fire for their God, some water, others the wind, and that under the names of Vulcan, Jupiter, and Neptune, and countless others.
</margin>
**2** But they hold for gods the fire, or the wind, or the swift stars, or the mighty water, or the lights in the heavens that rule the world.

<margin>
3 One may recognize physically how great the glory, power, and beauty must be in God, since these same gifts show themselves so clearly in the creatures, which are the works of His hands.
</margin>
**3** If they now took pleasure in the beautiful form of these things and thus held them for gods, they should rightly have known how much better He is who is Lord over such things: for He who is the master of all beauty has created all this.

<margin>
c Romans 1:21.
4 Thus they cannot raise their understanding above vain appearances.
</margin>
**4** And if they wondered at their power and strength, they should rightly have noticed from the same how much more powerful He is who has prepared all these things.

**5** For from the great beauty and the works, the Master of the same can be known, as if in an image.

**6** However, concerning these, it is not so entirely to be lamented: for they may also go astray while seeking God and wishing to find Him.

**7** For as they deal with His creation and reflect upon it, they are captured by the sight, because the creatures which are seen are so beautiful.

**8** Yet they are not thereby excused.

**9** For if they were able to know so much that they could highly esteem the creatures: why did they not much sooner find the Lord of the same?

<margin>
5 This is another species of idolatry: the first held the beautiful creatures and works of God as Gods; these make a God from the work of their hands.
d Acts 17:29.
e Isaiah 44:12, 46:4.
Jeremiah 10:3, 51:17.
</margin>
**10** But those are the unhappy ones, and whose hope is rightly to be counted among the dead, who call the handiwork of men "God": such as gold and silver prepared with art, and the images of animals, or useless stones made in years of old.

**11** As when a carpenter, seeking some work to do, cuts down a tree somewhere, and trims and shapes it well, making something artistic and fine from it, which is used for the necessities of life.

<margin>
f Isaiah 44:17.
</margin>
**12** The chips from such labor he then uses to cook food, so that he may be full.

**13** And what remains of it, which is thus not useful, being crooked wood and full of knots, he takes and carves it—when he has nothing else to do—with diligence, and fashions it masterfully according to his art:

<margin>
g Jeremiah 10:4.
h Habakkuk 3:14.
i Isaiah 2:8.
</margin>
**14** And makes it like the image of a man, or a despised animal, and colors it with red and white paint, red and beautiful, and where there is a blemish, he smears it over.

<margin>
6 Thus far he has recounted the form, the madness, and the lack of understanding of those who make the images; and of the idol-worshippers being used; now he goes on to describe the madness of those who pray to them, and shows that there is nothing else but vanity and folly when compared with wisdom.
</margin>
**15** And makes a fine little house for it, and sets it on the wall, and fastens it tightly with iron so that it does not fall; thus he provides for it well.

**16** For he knows that it cannot help itself: for it is an image, and indeed needs help.

**17** And when he prays for his goods, for his wife, for his children, he is not ashamed to speak with a lifeless thing.

Sapientia,
1
<meta>catchword: life</meta>

<margin>
1 He who knows himself to be among the number of the elect will not be lost; yet he does not use this as an excuse to sin, but rather keeps himself from evil and remains in the fear of the Lord, who through the grace of the Spirit confirms that he is a child of God.
a Psalm 103:8. Jonah 4:2. John 17:3.
2 He speaks here of the salvific knowledge of God which is united with faith, of which Christ speaks in John 17: "This is eternal life, that they [know] You," etc.
3 By which they have fashioned and made false gods.
d Romans 9:20. Isaiah 45:9. Jeremiah 18:3. e Genesis 2:7 / 3:19. f Luke 12:20.
4 The soul, through which the parts of the earthly body receive life, is given to us as if in safekeeping, to be given back again to the one who breathed it into us whenever it pleases Him; therefore, that returning is not in our power, but we are commanded to guard it faithfully.
g Isaiah 44:12 / 46:5. h Genesis 2:7.
5 He means to say that such a person's feeling is that it is all over for a man when he is removed from this mortal body, without them having any consideration for the future life.
6 That is: he lets them think that they have received this life only to gather temporal goods, and to practice thriftiness to acquire earthly things.
7 Namely: The potters, mentioned above in verses 7 and 8.
8 By "the dull" he signifies those who are alienated from the knowledge of God and run to mute idols.
i Psalm 115:5 / 135:16. Revelation 19:20. k Wisdom 13:10. Jeremiah 10:5.
9 God alone is the one who gives life through the Spirit of quickening; therefore, if they had any life or faith in them, they would worship their own craftsman, and that with good right; thus it is a hideous thing that man worships an image which is the work of his own hands.
l Such as dragons, serpents, cats, and similar animals.
</margin>

...not / for we are counted as Yours.
3 <margin>b</margin> For to know You <margin>c</margin> is perfect righteousness: and to know Your power is the root of eternal life.
4 For the evil <margin>d</margin> inventions of men did not so deceive us, nor the useless labor of painters / namely / a multicolored image, with many kinds of colors.
5 The form of which provokes the senseless: and those who gladly do evil also have their lust for that lifeless and dead image.
6 They are also worthy of such fruit, both those who make them, desire them, and honor them.
7 <margin>e</margin> And a potter, who works the soft clay with effort, makes all kinds of vessels for our use: and he makes from the same clay both vessels that serve for clean and also those that serve for unclean works: and what each of them shall be used for, that is determined by the potter.
8 Yet, it is a wretched labor when he makes a worthless god from the same clay, <margin>f</margin> though he himself was made from earth not long before, and after a little time returns thither from whence he was taken, <margin>g</margin> when the soul, which he used, is taken from him.
9 Yet his concern is not that he labors, nor that he has such a short life: <margin>h</margin> but that he works in competition with the goldsmiths and silversmiths, and that he may imitate the brass-founders: and he considers it a glory that he makes false work.
10 For the thoughts of his heart are like ashes, and his hope more base than earth, and his life more despised than clay:
11 Because he does not know Him who made him, and breathed into him the soul that works within him, and blew into him the living breath.
12 They also hold human life to be a mockery, and human existence to be a <margin>6</margin> marketplace <note>The original Dutch *iaermarct* refers to a yearly fair or trade festival, suggesting life is seen only as an opportunity for profit.</note>: claiming one must seek profit everywhere, even through evil deeds.
13 These <margin>7</margin> know above all that they sin, when they make such vain things and images from earthly clay.
14 They are indeed <margin>8</margin> duller and more wretched than a child / namely the enemies of Your people, whom they oppress.
15 For they <margin>i</margin> hold all kinds of idols of the heathens for gods, <margin>k</margin> whose eyes do not see, nor their noses draw breath, nor their ears hear, nor can the fingers on their hands feel, <margin>l</margin> and their feet are entirely lame for walking.

### The 16th Chapter.

->*1. The punishment of idolaters is just: / 2. and God has given His people a rare food / 6. God gave the children of Israel a healing sign / 8. God delivers from all evil / 11. God punishes His own, so that they should remember Him: 12. and the word of the Lord, 13. God has power over both life and death / 15. it is impossible to flee the hand of the Lord / 24. 1 THEREFORE they were justly plagued with the likes of themselves, <margin>a</margin> and were tortured by the multitude of evil worms.
2 Against which plague You did good to Your people, <margin>b</margin> and prepared for them a rare food, namely: Quails, for nourishment, after which they lusted.
3 So that those who lusted after such <margin>c</margin> food, through such given and sent quails, also learned to break away from natural necessity: the others now, who had suffered distress for a short time, <margin>4</margin> partook also of a new food.
4 For it was to be so, that such distress should happen to those who acted tyrannically, which could not be stopped: yet to these [Israelites] only a lesson occurred as to how their enemies were plagued.
5 Truly upon these also came <margin>d</margin> evil angry beasts, and they were bitten and destroyed by the crooked snakes.
6 Yet the anger did not remain forever, but they were terrified for a short time as a warning: for they had a <margin>e</margin> healing sign, so that they might remember the commandment of Your law.
7 For those who turned toward the same sign were made healthy, not by that which they looked upon, but by You, the Savior of all.
8 And therein You also proved to our enemies that You are the helper from all evil.
9 <margin>f</margin> But those were stung to death by locusts and flies, and found no help for their lives: for they were worthy to be plagued therewith.
10 But the venomous dragon teeth could not harm Your children: for Your mercy was there for them and made them healthy.
11 For they were punished in this way and quickly helped again, so that they might learn to remember Your words, and not fall too deep into forgetfulness, but remain unswerving from Your benefits.
12 For no herb or plaster healed them, but <margin>g</margin> Your word, Lord, which heals all things.
13 <margin>h</margin> For You have power over both life and death.

> 8 This was the metal serpent, through which it is prefigured that we are delivered by Christ from the venomous bite of Satan and instructed in the law of the Lord.

> f That is: because they believed Your word; for they well acknowledged that the serpent was a dead creature without feeling, and that it therefore did not have the power of healing from within itself, but because they looked upon the ordinance of God through faith alone, they obtained health.

# ECCLESIASTICVS,
## IESVS SYRACH.

->Preface of Jesus Sirach to his book.<-

**M**any and great men have made wisdom known to us through the Law, the Prophets, and others who followed them. For these things, Israel must be rightly praised for their wisdom and teaching. Therefore, those who have and read them should not only become wise themselves but also serve others by teaching and writing. My grandfather Jesus, after he had especially applied himself to reading the Law, the Prophets, and the other books left to us by our fathers, and had practiced well therein, intended also to write something concerning wisdom and good morals, so that those who were eager to learn and become bold might become even more understanding and fit to lead a good life. Therefore I pray you, that you will receive it kindly and read it with diligence, and hold us in good stead if we cannot speak as well as the great and famous orators. For what is written in the Hebrew language does not sound as well when one brings it into another language. Not only this my book, but also the Law, the Prophets, and other books sound quite differently when they are spoken in their own language. When I came into Egypt, in the thirty-eighth year, during the time of King Ptolemy Euergetes, and remained there during his lifetime, I found the opportunity to read and write many good things. Therefore I considered it good and necessary that I should apply diligence and effort to it and translate this book. And while I had the time, I labored and applied diligence to finish this book and bring it to light: so that the strangers also, who wish to learn, may accustom themselves to those morals, that they may live according to the Law of the Lord.

1 Do not rely on your wealth, and do not think: I have enough for myself.
2 Do not follow your wantonness, even if you are fully capable of it, and do not do whatever you please.
3 And do not think: Who will prevent it? For the Lord, the supreme avenger, will avenge it.
4 Do not say: I have sinned before, and no evil has happened to me; for the Lord is patient, yet He shall not leave you unpunished.
5 And do not be so secure because your sin is not yet punished, that you would therefore always continue to sin.
6 Do not think either: God is entirely merciful, He will not punish me, I may sin as much as I want.
7 He can become as angry in a short time as He is merciful, and His wrath over the godless has no end.
8 Therefore, do not delay in turning to the Lord, and do not put it off from one day to the next.
9 For His wrath comes very suddenly, and He shall avenge it and destroy you.
10 Do not rely on unrighteous goods: for they do not help you when temptations shall come.
11 Do not let yourself be carried by every wind, and do not follow every way, as the inconstant hearts do.
12 But be steadfast in your word, and remain with one single reason.
13 Be ready to hear, and answer what is right, and do not hurry yourself.
14 If you understand the matter, then instruct your neighbor; if not, then keep your mouth shut.
15 For speaking brings honor, and speaking also brings shame; and man brings his own tongue to its fall.
16 Do not be a whisperer <note>original: "oorenblaser"; literally "ear-blower," a talebearer</note>, and do not be a backbiter with your tongue.
17 A thief is a shameful thing, but a backbiter is much more shameful.
18 Do not consider it a small matter, whether it be little or great.

## Chapter 11.

<margin>a Genesis 41:40. Daniel 6:3. Psalm 113:7. 1 This was shown in Joseph among the Egyptians and in Daniel among the Persians.</margin>
1 **T**he wisdom of the lowly brings him to honor and sets him among the Princes.

<margin>2 The qualities of the body do not make a person good or bad, but rather the disposition of the heart. 3 By this he wishes to prove that one must not despise anyone because of the greatness or smallness of their physical stature.</margin>
2 You shall praise no one for the sake of their grand appearance: nor despise anyone for the sake of their lowly appearance.
3 For a bee is a tiny creature <note>original: "voghelken" - literally "little bird," an archaic way of describing small flying creatures</note> and yet gives the very sweetest fruit.

<margin>b Acts 12:21. 4 If any honor is shown to you. 5 That is: in the place of tyrants, they have been chosen as regents.</margin>
4 **Do not** exalt yourself because of your clothing, and do not be bold in your honor: for the Lord is wonderful in his works, and no one knows what he intends to do.
5 Many tyrants have had to sit down upon the earth, and the crown has been placed upon those of whom one had not even thought.
6 Many great Lords have come to nothing, and powerful Kings have been given into the hands of others.

<margin>c 1 Samuel 15:26. Esther 6:10 / 7:10. 6 By this he makes it known that people in this world are subject to many changes.</margin>
7 Condemn no one before you understand the matter: understand it first, and then punish.
8 You shall not judge before you hear the matter, and let the people speak their fill first.
9 Do not involve yourself in strange matters, and do not sit by an unjust judgment.

<margin>d Deuteronomy 13:14 / 17:6. Joshua 7:13 / 22:13. John 7:51. e Proverbs 18:13. 7 We must maintain this rule unless the matter concerns the honor of God, the salvation of our neighbor, or ourselves in particular; in such cases, we may indeed involve ourselves. 8 By this he wishes to teach us that we must act with foresight, and to gain wealth, we should not involve ourselves in many kinds of business, for that cannot easily happen without abandoning justice.</margin>
10 My child, do not involve yourself in many kinds of business: for if you undertake too many things, you shall not gain much from them.
11 Even if you strive greatly for it, you still will not achieve it: and even if you flit here and there, you still will not escape.
12 There is many a man who lets it be hard for him, and hastens toward riches, and only hinders himself thereby.

<margin>9 Otherwise, you shall remain stuck under the burden. f Job 42:10. g Job 42:12. h Job 1:12. Lamentations 3:37. Ezekiel 18:4. 10 One cannot say that God is the author of wickedness, but rather that evil comes from the Lord because it happens through his providence; nonetheless, the corrupt quality is solely in the human who does it. To clarify this, consider this example: God in his counsel ordained that through the death of his son, humanity should be brought to the hope of eternal life; this served us and showed unfathomable love, but those who killed Christ committed a gruesome sin.</margin>
13 On the other hand, there is many a man who takes things slowly: who indeed needs help, is weak and poor, yet God looks upon him with grace and helps him out of misery, and brings him to honor, so that many wonder at it.
14 15 16 It all comes from God: good luck and bad luck, life and death, poverty and riches.
17 God gives good things to the godly, which remain, and whatever he undertakes, that always prospers.
18 There is many a man who is stingy and saves, and becomes rich thereby:
19 And thinks he has secured something for himself, and says: Now I will have a good life, eating and drinking from my goods.
20 And he does not know that his hour is so near, and he must leave it all to others and die.
21 Stay with God’s word, and exercise yourself therein, and remain in your calling.
22 Do not let it wonder you that the godless strive for success; trust you in God, and remain in your calling.
23 For it is very easy for the Lord to make a poor man rich.
24 God blesses the goods of the godly, and when the time comes, they prosper quickly.

<margin>i Psalm 39:7. Psalm 49:18. 2 Peter 1:10. m Luke 12:19. 1 Timothy 6:7. n Job 1:21 / 27:19. o Matthew 10:16, 38. p Ephesians 2:7. Sirach 5:14. Ephesians 4:3. 11 That is: keep yourself content with your condition, and do not desire a higher station. 12 One must not wonder that the wicked live in prosperity, nor be moved thereby to deviate from a godly calling. q Job 42:10. 13 By this he wishes to make known that man should not fix his eyes on that which is fleeting, but on God who is a fountain of all good, and who can send us all good at the proper time, and when it is for our salvation.</margin>
25 Do not say: What does it help me, and what do I have in the meantime?

<column-break/>

<margin>r Sirach 18:25.</margin>
26 Do not say: I have enough, how can I lack anything?
27 When things go well for you, think that they can go badly for you again: and when things go badly for you, think that they can go well for you again.

<margin>14 One should not rely on anything that changes; what is fixed remains, for what is to come remains. f Jeremiah 17:10. Psalm 28:4 / 62:13. Job 34:11. Matthew 16:27. Romans 2:6. 2 Corinthians 5:10. Revelation 2:23. 15 The end of life testifies to what kind of life we have led. 16 If someone leaves behind good children, that is proof that he also was good; and on the contrary, if he leaves behind willful and disobedient children—though it often happens otherwise, namely, that children may depart from the good nature of the father. 17 He who often trusts another without suspicion is deceived by his cunning, just as a decoy bird brings other birds into the net. t James 3:5. 18 By this he does not wish to forbid us from harboring strangers in our house, as Abraham, Lot, and other holy fathers did, but that we should be cautious in it, so that we do not reveal our secrets to them, so that no unrest comes upon us.</margin>
28 For the Lord can easily repay every person in death, just as he has deserved it.
29 An evil hour makes one forget all joy: and when a person dies, he becomes aware of how he has lived.
30 Therefore you shall praise no one before his end: for what kind of godly man someone was, that is found in his descendants.
31 Do not harbor just anyone in your house: for the world is full of unfaithfulness and cunning.
32 A false heart is just like a decoy bird in a trap, and it lurks to see how it might catch you.
33 For whatever good he sees, he interprets it in the very worst way, and the very best he slanders to the highest degree.
34 From a single spark, a great fire grows, and the godless man does not stop until he sheds blood.
35 Guard yourself against such scoundrels: they have nothing good in mind, so that they do not attach an eternal shame to you.
36 If you take a stranger in with you, he will cause you unrest and drive you out of your own property.
