## The xiij. Chapter.

1. Do not mix with the proud, 2. nor with the company of the powerful and rich, 4. etc. 25. the rich are carried and helped up, and the poor are pushed down, 10. do not let yourself be deceived by simplicity, 12. how one should behave with the powerful, 19. every creature keeps to its own kind, 21. the godless have no similarity to the pious, 23. the poor are the fodder of the rich, 30. wealth is good.

<margin>Chapter xiij.
1 Hereby he gives it to be understood that one cannot associate with the wicked without being infected by their wickedness. a Deuteronomy 7:2.</margin>
1 Who touches pitch is defiled by it: and who has company with the proud learns pride.
<margin>2 D. Do not meddle in that which is above your power.</margin>
<margin>3 The metal pot is the powerful one, who wishes to strike the earthen pot—that is, the poor and small—into pieces.</margin>
<margin>4 While the rich man is driven by greed, he desires no fellowship with his neighbors, except when he expects many things and assistance from them.</margin>
2 Do not mark your company with the powerful and rich, otherwise you load a heavy burden upon yourself.
3 What should the earthen pot do by the metal pot? For if they strike against one another, it breaks.
4 The rich man does wrong and boasts besides, but the poor man must suffer and thank him for it.
<margin>5 Others: That you do not waste your wisdom: although the Lord richly endows many people through His grace, they nevertheless let those same gifts remain hidden and do not bring them into the light, fearing that they might thereby forget themselves through boldness and cling to pride; but such people waste their wisdom and are deceived through their simplicity.</margin>
5 As long as you are useful to him, he uses you: but when you can do no more, he lets you go.
6 While you have something, he consumes it with you, and it does not trouble him that you are ruined.
7 When he needs you, he can deceive you, and smiles at you, promises you much, and gives you the best words, and says: Do you need anything?
8 And invites you once or thrice deceitfully as a guest, until he brings you to lose what is yours, and finally mocks you: and even if he clearly sees your need, he still lets you go and shakes his head over you.
10 11 !! Therefore see to it that your simplicity does not deceive you and bring you into misfortune.
<margin>7 Hereby he commands that we should keep a middle measure in this: that is, not to push ourselves forward too hastily, nor also to refuse fellowship with them too much.</margin>
12 When a powerful man wants to draw you to him, then refuse, so shall he draw you to him all the more.
13 Do not push yourself upon him, so that you are not cast out: do not withdraw yourself too much either, so that one may use you in case of need.
14 Do not refuse if he commands you anything: but do not rely on it that he makes himself so common with you: for he tempts you therewith, and with his friendly face, he draws you out.
15 But if he becomes unmerciful, then it does not stop at such friendly words, and he does not mock with punishments and imprisonment.

<column-break/>

17 18 !! Therefore guard yourself, and look well before you; live in great fear.
<margin>8 By these following parables he wishes to prove that just as there is always an irreconcilable conflict between righteousness and wickedness, so also the persons who are endowed with wisdom and understanding—that is, with the choice of the way of righteousness—should not become similar in essence to the godless, since even the irrational creatures do not join themselves except to their own kind. b 2 Corinthians 6:14.</margin>
19 20 Every creature keeps to its own kind, so shall a person also join himself to his like.
21 !! It is just as when a wolf joins the sheep, when a godless man joins the pious.
22 Just as the hyena makes fellowship with the dog, so also the rich with the poor.
<margin>9 Others: What fellowship has a serpent with the dog, etc. Because a serpent creeps upon the earth, the humility and lowliness of the poor is thereby depicted.</margin>
<margin>10 The rich and powerful are here compared to three beasts: namely, the wolf, the dog, and the lion, because of the similar qualities seen in them and the aforementioned animals; for he is like a wolf while [devouring] the poor, like a dog [in persistence], and proudly subjects others like a lion. c Psalm 60.</margin>
23 Just as the * lion devours the game in the heath, so the rich devour the poor.
24 Just as the proud man despises what is lowly, so is the poor man also despised by the rich.
25 When the rich man is about to fall, his friends help him up: when the poor man falls, his friends push him down.
26 When a rich man has not done right, there are many who gloss it over: when he has transgressed with words, one must let it be right.
27 But when a poor man has not done right, one considers it a great matter, and even if he speaks wisely, it nonetheless finds no place.
28 When the rich man speaks, everyone is silent, and his word is raised to the heavens.
29 But when the poor man speaks, then they say: who is that? and if he trips, he must pay for it.
30 Riches are indeed good if one uses them without sin, but the poverty of the godless teaches much evil speaking.
31 What one has in mind can be seen in their eyes, whether it be good or evil.
<margin>11 D. If one uses them for what is right, as the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob have done; therefore riches and poverty are not in themselves evil or good, but as the person is, so they are also.
a Psalm 1:1.
Sirach 19:16, 25:11.
James 3:2.</margin>
32 If he has something good in mind, he looks cheerful: but whoever deals in secret matters can have no rest for them.

## The xiiij. Chapter.

1. Blessed is he who gives no evil counsel, 2. nor has an evil conscience, 6. and 8. an envious person who grants nothing good to himself or others, 9. an insatiable person, 10. an envious person, 12. death does not tarry, 13. doing good before one's end, 18. all flesh withers, 19. the generation of men, 22. blessed is he who occupies all his rest with God's word.

<margin>Chapter xiiij.
1 This is what James writes, chapter 3, verse 2, about stumbling in the word.</margin>
1 **B**lessed is he who gives no evil counsel, and has no evil conscience from it.
<margin>2 Others: Who is not grieved by sin, etc. that is, who has no evil conscience, and having well examined themselves, finds no cause for any gnawing within them; for otherwise there is a sorrow toward God when a person finds themselves to be a sinner and, having a dislike for it, turns themselves to God.</margin>
2 Blessed is he who has no evil conscience, and whose confidence has not failed him.
<margin>3 Others: An envious one, and rightly calls the miser a disgraced person: envious, because he does not even sustain himself during the days of his own life.</margin>
3 Wealth does not suit a miser: and what use are gold and goods to * a greedy dog?
4 Whoever gathers much and does nothing good for himself, gathers it for other people, and other people shall squander it.
5 Whoever does nothing good for himself, to what other people would he do good? He never becomes joyful from his goods.
6 There is no more shameful thing than one who grants himself nothing good, and that is the right plague for his wickedness.
7 If he does something good, he certainly knows nothing of it, and finally becomes impatient about it.
<margin>b Jeremiah 17:11.
Luke 12:15.
4 Others: because love—faith through love—is powerful, being well-wishing to one's neighbor; so also to the contrary, he who is driven only to his own profit through greed brings his neighbor all evil.</margin>
8 That is an * evil person, who will not look upon the goods for the maintenance of temporal life, and refuses to use them.

<meta>This page continues the wisdom of Jesus Sirach, specifically Chapter 29 on the ethics of lending and Chapter 30 on the discipline of children. It follows the previous discussion on social conduct and guarding secrets.</meta>

Fol. 134.
# Jesus Sirach.

### Column 1

<margin>
**Chapter xxix.**
1 It is indeed true that lending is spoken of here / but this same principle also applies to all other acts of kindness that we must show one another in times of need. **a Deut. 15:7, Luke 6:30.**
2 He admonishes those here who borrow from their neighbor / that they must faithfully keep their promises to return what was given. **b Eccles. 8:15.**
3 Some cannot bear to have what they borrowed legally demanded back / he intends to address this in these two verses.
4 When he pays his creditor half of what he borrowed / he lets himself think that he is showing him a great friendship.
5 He has often subjected himself to many snares and perils / he who is a debtor turns his back on the hope that if the creditor dies / he would not have to pay him.
6 Although we are all together bound to give our neighbor all help and assistance in times of need / it is nevertheless commendable to use foresight / and not to be reckless / regarding for what reason / and to whom we lend our goods. **c Deut. 15:7, Luke 6:35.**
7 He means to say: help your neighbor rather with your goods / than to let them rot under the earth / which rust shall bear witness on the day of righteous judgment against those who have abandoned their neighbor. **d Matt. 6:20, Luke 12:33, 1 Tim. 6:19, Tobit 4:11.**
8 The commandment of the Lord is that we shall gather for ourselves a treasure in heaven: that is: to give all assistance to the needy, **Matt. 6:20.** **e Daniel 4:26.** **Luke 11:41, Acts 10:2.**
9 Another reading: Shut up mercy in your secret treasuries / etc. Just as you secretly shut your earthly treasures in your vaults / to preserve them / so you must lay away a good treasure for the future / and do so secretly. Give your alms so / that the left hand does not know what the right hand deals out, **Matt. 6.**
10 Since true alms spring from faith / which is powerful through love / so love is often credited with / what properly belongs to faith / therefore they are also said to deliver us from eternal death / and all misfortune.
11 He who becomes a guarantor for his neighbor / puts himself in great peril / therefore Solomon often advises for the best / that we shall not become a guarantor for another / in which we must nevertheless regulate ourselves according to what was said before, **Prov. 6:5.**
12 That is: Many have lost all their goods / because they had become a guarantor for another.
</margin>

# Chapter xxix.

He who lends to his neighbor / performs a work of mercy: and he who has means / shall do so.
2 Lend to your neighbor / when he has need: and you in turn / give it back at the appointed time.
3 Keep what you have spoken / and do not deal deceitfully with him / so you will find what you need at all times.
4 Many think / that what they borrow is a found object: and they make trouble for him / who has helped them.
5 He kisses one's hand / while he is being lent to / and speaks so humbly of the neighbor's money.
6 But when he is to give it back / then he delays / and complains greatly / that it is a hard time.
7 And even if he is well able / he still barely gives half back / and counts that to the other as a gain.
8 If he is not able / then he brings the other to ruin regarding the money: the same has bought himself an enemy / with his own money.
9 And the debtor pays him with cursing and reviling / and gives him spiteful words instead of money.
10 Many lend unwillingly / not out of any evil intention / but they must fear / that they will lose what is theirs.
11 But have patience with your neighbor in need / and give alms besides / so that you give him time.
12 Help the poor / for the sake of the commandment: and in his need do not let him go from you empty-handed.
13 Gladly lose your money for your brother and neighbor’s sake / and do not bury it under a stone / where it will surely perish.
14 <margin>d **Matt. 6:20, Luke 12:33, 1 Tim. 6:19, Tobit 4:11.**</margin> d Gather for yourself a treasure / according to the commandment of the Most High: <margin>e **Daniel 4:26.**</margin> that shall be better for you / than any gold.
15 16 Store your alms / in a special place: that same act shall deliver you from all misfortune.
17 18 It shall fight for you against your enemy / better than any shield or spear.
19 A pious man becomes a guarantor <note>A "borg" or guarantor is someone who legally promises to pay another person's debt if they fail to do so.</note> for his neighbor: but a shameless person / leaves his guarantor stranded.
20 Do not forget the kindness of your guarantor: for he has put himself forward for you.
21 22 The ungodly person brings his guarantor to harm: and an ungrateful person leaves his redeemer stuck.
23 24 Becoming a guarantor / has ruined many rich people / and tossed them to and fro / like the waves in the sea.
25 It has driven away great people / so that

they had to go wandering in foreign lands.

# The xxx. Chapter.

*1. His child-discipline / 8. a spoiled child / 14. a poor man in good health / 15. no gold is better than health / 18. and 19. the offering is useless to idols / 23. one shall do good to oneself / 25. envy and strife shorten life / 26. a cheerful heart.*

He who loves his child / keeps him always under the rod / so that he may hereafter experience joy in him. <margin>**Chap. xxx. a Prov. 13:24 / 23:13.**</margin>
2 He who chastises his child / shall rejoice over him / and need not be ashamed because of him among acquaintances.
3 When one instructs his child / that <margin>**b Deut. 6:7.**</margin> vexes his enemy / and gladdens his friends.
4 For if his father dies / it is as if he had not died: for he has left behind one like himself.
5 While he lived he saw his delight / and had joy in him / when he died / he did not need to worry.
6 For he has left behind a protector against his enemies / and one who can serve his friends in return.
7 But he who is too soft with his children / <margin>1 By this he makes known / that he who may not chastise his child / denies him the medicine / with which his wounds could be healed.</margin> shall bandage their stripes / and be startled as often as the child weeps.
8 A spoiled child / becomes headstrong / just like a wild horse.
9 Pamper your child / then you must hereafter fear him: play with him / then he shall hereafter make you grieve.
10 Do not joke with him / so that you do not have to mourn with him hereafter / and gnash your teeth at the last. <margin>2 Since the nature of children is evil from youth onwards / it is necessary that they be tamed through proper chastisement / as if by a bridle. **c Sirach 7:25.**</margin>
11 Do not let him have his way in his youth / and do not excuse his folly.
12 Bend his neck / while it is still young / bruise his back / while it is still small: so that he does not become stubborn / and disobedient to you. <margin>3 That is: Bring him under your obedience / while he is still young / through persistent chastisement.</margin>
13 Instruct your child / and do not let him go idle / so that you do not come to shame because of him.
14 It is better / that one be poor / and in good health / and fit withal / than rich and unhealthy.

# Ecclesiasticus.

16 No riches can be compared to a healthy body: and no joy is equal to the joy of the heart.

<margin>**1 Timothy 6:9.** 1 For greed drives man to all unrighteousness, and keeps him caught in its snares until the end of his life to his great shame.</margin>

Fol. 135.
# Jesus Sirach.

<margin>1 He indicates that one should maintain good order when speaking certain words and diligently consider all circumstances so that no unseemliness is found, just as happens with musical instruments when they do not accord with one another.</margin>
<margin>a Ecclesiastes 3:7, Sirach 20:7.</margin>
5 The elder shall speak, for it belongs to him as one who is experienced: and do not hinder the musicians.

6 And when songs are sung, do not chatter, and save your wisdom for another time.

<margin>2 A precious stone illuminates the gold and is itself adorned by it: just as the music and string-play adorn the feast, and the feast is itself adorned by them; yet the wise man here does not speak of feasts intended for the pleasures of the flesh with all the noise of stringed instruments, of which Isaiah chapter 5 speaks, but of those held with gratitude and manners, which were also in use among the saints of God in former times. b Job 32:6.</margin>
7 Just as a ruby shines in fine gold, so a song adorns the social gathering <note>original: "collatie" - a light meal or social meeting</note>.

8 9 Just as an emerald is set in beautiful gold, so do the songs adorn the good wine.

10 <insert>13</insert> A young man may also speak once or twice if it is necessary for him.

11 And when he is asked, he shall keep it brief, and conduct himself as one who does not know much, and would rather remain silent.

12 And he shall not consider himself equal to the lords: and when an old man speaks, do not interrupt.

13 14 Thunder makes great lightning; modesty creates great favor.

15 Rise also in good time, and be not the last to leave, but go quickly home.

16 And play there, and do what you wish: provided that you do nothing evil, and boast to no one.

17 But thank for all this Him who created you and has satisfied you with His goods.

<margin>3 Two things the wise man teaches us here, by which God is tempted: first, that one should not meddle with difficult things that are beyond our ability. Secondly, that one should not take pleasure in oneself with a vain trust, as if our power were so great that we could not stumble; for this is against the nature of true faith, which does nothing flippantly nor with a trust in creatures, but regulates itself according to the contents of God's Word.</margin>
18 Whoever fears the Lord willingly allows himself to be instructed: and whoever prepares himself early for it shall find grace.

19 Whoever inquires after God's Word shall receive it abundantly: whoever does not mean it with earnestness shall only be made worse by it.

20 Whoever fears the Lord finds the right teaching, and makes righteousness shine like a light.

21 A godless man does not allow himself to be punished: and knows how to help himself by using the example of other people in his intentions.

22 23 A prudent man does not despise good counsel: but a wild and proud person fears nothing, no matter what he has done.

24 Do nothing without counsel: so you will not regret it after the deed.

25 Do not go the way where you might fall, nor where you might strike yourself against the stones: do not rely on the way being level.

26 Indeed, watch yourself even before your own children.

27 Whatever you undertake, trust God with your whole heart: for that is keeping God's commandment.

28 And whoever trusts the Lord shall lack nothing.

### The 33rd Chapter.

## Chap. XXXII.

<margin>a Ecclesiastes 1:19.</margin>
1 Whoever fears God, no evil happens to him; but when he is tempted, he shall be delivered again.

2 A wise man does not let God's Word lead him astray: but a hypocrite wavers like a ship on the raging sea.

<margin>1 Just as a ship is driven on all sides between the waves of the sea, so also is the heart of a hypocrite; for when the law of God is set before him, he is troubled and trembles, and can find no rest of conscience.</margin>
3 An understanding person holds fast to God's Word, and God's Word is certain to him, like a clear reason.

<column-break/>

4 Become certain of the matter, then speak of it: let yourself be well taught beforehand, so you may answer.

<margin>b Sirach 21:17.</margin>
<margin>2 He means to say that the heart of the fool is always unstable and turns like a wheel.</margin>
5 The fool’s heart is like a wheel on a wagon, and his thoughts run around like the hub.

<margin>3 He fits all his reasons insatiably to all the desires of men.</margin>
6 Just as a stallion neighs against every mare: so the hypocrite clings to all mockers.

7 And speaks: Why must one day be holier than another? Since the sun makes one day in the year as well as the others.

8 The wisdom of the Lord has thus distinguished them.

9 And He has thus ordained the seasons and the days.

<margin>4 Where some days are thus ordained for service, others are ordained so that man may then practice his labor. c Genesis 2:7.</margin>
10 He has chosen and sanctified some above other days.

12 Some He has blessed, exalted, and chosen for His service, and some He has cursed and humbled, and thrust down from their seat.

<margin>d Isaiah 45:9, Jeremiah 18:6, Wisdom 15:13, Romans 9:20.</margin>
<margin>5 Although some men remain in a state of being cursed, nevertheless the righteousness of God is proven in everything; the fault lies solely in man that all the works of God are perverted in him, for it is always found true that when God and man work together, the work that has come forth perfectly from God's side is corrupted and made unclean by human nature.</margin>
13 For they are in His hand, like the clay in the potter's hand: He makes all His works as it pleases Him.

14 So also are men in the hand of Him who made them, and He gives to each as it seems good to Him.

<margin>e 2 Corinthians 6:14.</margin>
<margin>6 This teaches in spirituality and strength the sorrow, poverty and wealth, punishment of the author of good things of virtue.</margin>
15 Thus is good set against evil, and life against death, and the godly against the godless.

16 Thus look at all the works of the Most High, they are always two against two, and one ordained against the other.

17 I am the last to wake up, like one who gleans after the vintage, and God has given me the blessing so that I have also filled my winepress, as in the full autumn.

18 See how I have not labored for myself alone, but for all those who were willing to learn.

<margin>With this, the author of the book wishes to make known that he has given kindness through the enlightenment of the Spirit when some unwise and sharp-minded questions are asked by some people regarding the election of men.</margin>

20 Let not your son, wife, brother, or friend have power over you while you live, and give your goods to no one: so that you do not regret it and have to beg for them.

21 While you live and have breath, do not subject yourself to any other person.

22 It is better that your children have need of you, than that you must look to their hands.

<margin>f Sirach 24:47, g Sirach 9:7.</margin>
<margin>8 He counsels us that we should diligently strive to keep the ownership of our goods throughout our lives.</margin>
23 Remain the master of your goods, and do not let your honor be taken from you.

24 When your end comes, that you must depart, only then distribute your inheritance.

<margin>9 Whether they shall give you anything. h Genesis 48:12, i 1 Maccabees 1:7, i Sirach 42:26.</margin>
25 Fodder, a whip, and a burden belong to the donkey: so also bread, punishment, and labor belong to the servant.

26 Keep the servant at work, and you shall have rest from him: if you let him go idle, he will want to be a young lord.

27 The yoke and the thongs bow the neck: for an evil servant, the stocks and clubs.

<margin>10 This has no place in our time, in which one finds no slaves or persons of a servile condition.</margin>
28 Point him to work, so that he is not idle: idleness teaches much evil.

29 Impose labor upon him as befits a servant: if he does not then obey you, put him in the stocks.

## The 34th Chapter.

*1. Unwise people deceive themselves. 2. Paying attention to dreams. 5. and 6. > 1. He who shall teach the law of the Most High, 7. shall pray for the sins of all the people, 8. and 9. shall be gifted with the spirit of wisdom from the Lord, 10. and the Lord gives grace so that his counsel and teaching may proceed, 11. and he proves it with the holy scripture, 12. and 13. he, nor his wisdom, shall ever be forgotten, 21. and 39. the works of the Lord are good, 23. what He does through His command is lovely, 29. Chap. xxxix.
1 Whoever wishes to serve in the office of authority must practice in God's word, so that his service and office may be fulfilled according to justice.
2 d. As he reads the service of famous men, he shall be taught by it to direct his own service after their example.
3 d. Through his wisdom, he shall be found fit to govern in the land.
a Exodus 32:11. Numbers 14:13. Ezra 9:6. 3 Esdras 8:76.

b Daniel 2:19.
c 3 Kings 10:7. <note>1 Kings 10:7 in modern Bibles.</note>

But he who shall give himself to this, to learn the law of the Most High, and to study the Prophets.
2 He must note the histories of famous men and reflect upon them, what they signify and teach.
3 He must learn spiritual proverbs and practice himself in deep reasoning.
4 He can then serve the Prince and be among the Lords.
5 He can allow himself to be sent into foreign lands: for he has tested what is good and what is not good among people.
6 And he thinks of how he shall rise early to seek the Lord who created him, and prays before the Most High.
7 He opens his mouth and prays for the sins of all the people.
8 And when the Lord is thus reconciled, He gives him the spirit of wisdom richly.
9 So that he can powerfully give wise counsel and teaching, <margin>b</margin> for which he thanks the Lord in his prayer.
10 And the Lord gives grace so that his counsel and teaching proceed, and he meditates upon it beforehand within himself.
11 Thereafter he speaks his counsel, and teaches, and proves it with the holy scripture.

24 The works of all men are before Him, and nothing is hidden from His eyes. <margin>9 Answer: Those who do not acknowledge Him. Since there is no nation in the world so barbaric and wild that is not convinced by all the glorious works of the world that there is a God who must be served, so it is rightly said in scripture that the Lord justly pours out His wrath upon those people when they do not show Him His due honor.</margin>

### The XL. Chapter.

1. Human life is a miserable and piteous thing; 2, 5. it is always beset with much suffering; 8. the godless suffer seven times more; 12. truth remains forever; 13. the goods of the godless; 15. the descendants of the godless; 18. he who supports himself through labor and is content; 19. an honorable wife; 20. the loveliness of wisdom; 21. a friendly word; 23. help in times of need; 26. the fear of the Lord; 29. and 32. begging; 30. and 31. he who relies on another’s table.

Ch. xl.
1 Man is by nature burdened in this life with spiritual and physical misery; the spiritual conditions are the powers of the soul; the physical is the oppression of the body: fear of death, anxiety, hunger, thirst, grief, sickness, labor. Furthermore, in the curse of the earth: in hail, snow, heavy tempests, which are all punishments for sin.

i Exodus 23:8. Deuteronomy 17:2. Proverbs 17:23. Sirach 20:31. Ezekiel 22:12.

1 Timothy 6:6. Sirach 29:29. Proverbs 15:16. Philippians 4:11.
6 One who is not content due to immoderate greed, keeping himself too busy with his trade.

n Wisdom 6:7, 8. Proverbs 8:1. Sirach 24:1.
o Proverbs 15:1 / 25:15.

It is a miserable, piteous thing with the lives of all men, from the mother’s womb until they are buried in the earth, which is the mother of us all.
2 There is always worry, fear, hope, and at last, death.
3 This is true for him who sits in high honor, as well as for the lowliest on earth.
4 As well for him who wears silk and a crown, as for him who wears a rough garment <note>original: "groven kedel," a coarse peasant's cowl or coat</note>.
5 There is always anger, jealousy, adversity, unrest, and fear of death, envy and strife; and when one should rest and sleep on his bed at night, many kinds of thoughts come to him.
6 Even if he rests a little, it is as nothing: for he is terrified in his dream, as if he saw enemies coming.
7 And when he wakes up and sees that he is safe, he feels like one who has escaped from the slaughter, and is exceedingly joyful that the fear was nothing.
8 Such things happen to all flesh, both to humans and to cattle: but to the godless seven times more.
9 Death, bloodshed, strife, sword, misfortune, hunger, destruction, and plague.
10 All such things are ordained against the godless: for because of them, the Great Flood had to come.
11 Everything that comes from the earth must return to the earth, just as all waters flow back into the sea.
12 All bribes and unrighteous goods must perish, but the truth remains forever.
13 The goods of the godless dry up like a brook, like the thunder departs in the rain.
14 They are joyful as long as they take gifts, but in the end they come to ruin.
15 The descendants of the godless shall not take root, and the root of the unrighteous stands on a bare stone.
16 Even if they stood by moisture and the water, they would be plucked up before they were ripe.
17 Yet, doing good is like a blessed garden, and mercy remains forever.
18 He who supports himself with his labor and is content has a fine, peaceful life: that is called finding a treasure above all treasures.
19 Begetting children and improving the city makes an eternal memory: but an honorable wife more than both of those.
20 Wine and stringed music gladden the heart: but wisdom is lovelier than both of those.
21 Pipes and harps sound well: but a friendly speech is better than both of those.
22 The eye loves to see what is lovely and beautiful: but a green sprout <note>likely referring to crops</note> more than both of those.

<column-break/>

<margin>
7 The more fruits of the fields that are seen in the seed, the more pleasant and lovely it is to our eyes.
p Genesis 14:14.
q Sirach 23:2.
r Psalm 41:1 / 112:5.
s James 2:13. Matthew 25:35.

</margin>

23 A friend comes to another in time of need: but a husband and wife much more.
24 A brother helps another in time of need: but mercy helps much more.
25 Gold and silver sustain a man: but good counsel much more.
26 Money and goods make one bold: but much more the fear of the Lord.
27 The fear of the Lord lacks nothing, and it needs no help.
28 The fear of the Lord is a blessed garden, and there is nothing as beautiful as it is.
29 My child, do not give yourself over to begging; it is better to die than to beg.
30 He who relies on another’s table does not think to support himself with honor:
31 For he must sin for the sake of strange food: but a sensible person guards himself against this.
32 Begging tastes good to the shameless mouth, but he shall at last get a wicked fever <term>original: "boose cortse," metaphorically a harsh consequence or the burning shame of poverty</term> from it.

<note>
"Shall at last get a wicked fever from it." That is, to force those who beg to labor and to forbid begging; if they are truly poor and sick, so that they cannot work, then their needs must be provided for. Therefore the Lord commanded His people in the Old Testament that no beggars should be found among them (Deuteronomy 15:4). Such a life is a type of beggary, for the mother of this is idleness, from which comes lack, and because of poverty comes begging.
</note>

### The XLI. Chapter.

<margin>Ch. xli.</margin>

1. The remembrance of death; 3. do not fear death; 6. and 7. no refusal helps against death; 8. the children of the godless; 11. woe unto the godless; 15. and 16. a good name; 17, 18, and 19. in prosperity one shall remain in the fear of God; 20. it is not good to be too shameful; 21. the things in which shame is to be praised.

<margin>
a Tobit 3:6. 1 Kings 19:4. Jonah 4:3.
1 The person who is entirely rooted in earthly and perishable things here, and lives in all happiness according to his will, cannot lift his heart to the covering of eternal life: and therefore it is an advantage to the godly that they are sometimes burdened with oppression, so that they may learn that there is nothing here but misery, and that our fatherland is in heaven.
2 That is: To those who have much grief in this life.
b Genesis 3:19. Sirach 3:3. Hebrews 9:27.
3 Therefore a person should always keep their eyes on the providence of God, through which He has set the time of death for man.
c Sirach 40:15.
d 2 Samuel 2:27.
e Genesis 3:19. Sirach 12:7 / 40:1.
</margin>

O Death, how bitter you are when a man thinks of you, who has good days and plenty.
2 And lives without worry, and for whom things go well in all matters, and who can still eat well.
3 O death, how well you do for the needy, who are weak and old.
4 Who are stuck in all kinds of worries, and have nothing better to hope for or expect.
5 Do not fear death.
6 Remember that it is thus ordained by the Lord over all flesh, both for those who were before you and those who shall come after you.
7 And why do you refuse the will of God, whether you live ten, a hundred, or a thousand years? For in death, one does not ask how long one has lived.
8 The children of the godless, and those who join themselves to the godless, become pure abominations.
9 The inheritance of the children of the godless perishes, and their descendants must be despised.
10 The children must complain about the godless father, for because of him they are despised.
11 Woe to you, godless ones, you who forsake the law of the Most High.
12 Whether you live or die, you people are cursed.
13 Just as everything that comes from the earth returns to the earth: so the godless come from the curse to damnation.
14 A person's suffering may last here as long as he lives: but the name of the godless must be rooted out: for it is worth nothing.
15 See to it that you keep a good name: that remains more certain than a thousand great treasures of gold.

<margin>
4 That is: The suffering of the godly is temporal, but that of the godless is eternal.
Proverbs 22:1. Sirach 7:2. Song of Solomon 1:3. 1 Maccabees 2:51.

# THE REMAINING PIECES OF THE BOOK OF ESTHER, FROM THE GREEK.

->Brief contents of this Book,<-

**S**ince a summary <note>original: "argument"</note> has been made for the book of Esther—which is among the number of books undoubtedly written by the Holy Spirit—it would be in vain to propose another summary here that would contain the same thing. Therefore, the reader may look through the aforementioned summary made for the book of Esther to understand what the history contains in brief.

**I**n the third year of the great King Artaxerxes, on the first day of the month of Nisan, <margin>a</margin> Mordecai—who was a Jew, a son of Jair, the son of Shimei, the son of Kish, of the tribe of Benjamin—had a dream:

# THE PROPHET
## BARUCH.

->Short summary of this Book.<-

Baruch, a faithful disciple and servant of the Prophet Jeremiah, wrote down all his prophecies, and everything he wished to bring to light from his godly teaching. After the destruction of Jerusalem and the carrying away of the people into Babylon, he remained with Jeremiah for a time in the land of the Jews, with some others of the people whom King Nebuchadnezzar had left there under the command of Gedaliah. When Gedaliah was deceased, Azariah, Johanan, and other powerful men took the people with them to Egypt, including Jeremiah and Baruch, against the advice Jeremiah had given them. Shortly thereafter, this same Baruch moved to Babylon after the death of Jeremiah, who was killed by some headstrong members of the people because he sternly rebuked them for their wickedness. As soon as he came to his captive brothers in Babylon, he wrote this book full of teaching and prophecy, which he had learned from his master Jeremiah, and read it publicly in the assembly of the Princes and elders of the people, recounting to them and the whole people the cause of their captivity, exhorting them to turn to the Lord with the improvement of their sinful lives, desiring that they should be fervent in prayer to God, and also assuring them that God would mercifully deliver them—just as Jeremiah had done before—if they did not give themselves over to the service of false idols.

### The 3rd Chapter.

->1. Prayer of the Jews, containing the confession of their sins; 9. exhortation to the Jews; 12. the Jews have forsaken the fountain of wisdom; 16. the Princes of this world have not found wisdom; 27. the Lord has not chosen the great ones of this world; 37. the Lord has bound wisdom.<-

<margin>
Cap. iij.
</margin>

ALmighty Lord, you God of Israel, in this great anguish and distress, I cry to you.
2 Hear, and be merciful, Lord: for we have sinned against you.
3 You rule from eternity to eternity, but we perish forever.

<margin>
a This is to say: Almighty God, you know that our patriarchs prayed to you, and that not only for themselves, but also for us their descendants, knowing the evil that we would commit through disobedience; therefore we pray you that you would be mindful of this.
</margin>

4 Almighty Lord, you God of Israel, hear now the prayer of Israel, who are at death's door <note>original: "den dooden inden halse steken" - literally "sticking the dead in the throat," an idiom for being in mortal peril or near death.</note>, and the prayer of those who have sinned against you and have not been obedient to the voice of the Lord their God, therefore the punishment has also remained behind us.
5 Do not think of the misdeeds of our fathers, but think now of your hand and of your name.
6 For you, Lord, are indeed our God, so we will praise you, Lord.
7 For you have given your fear into our hearts for this reason: that we should call upon your name and praise you in our captivity; for all the misdeeds of our fathers, who sinned before you, go to our hearts.
8 We who are now in our captivity, where you have cast us out for a reproach, a curse, and an abomination, for the sake of all the misdeeds of our fathers, who

<column-break/>

turned away from the Lord their God.

<margin>
2 He calls the Heathen "dead" because, though living, they are dead through the misdeeds of sin, and because they are far from the life that is in Christ.
3 To be counted among those who go down into hell is nothing else than to be deprived of the company of the believers, who in this life possess the hope of the future life through faith. a Jerem. 2:15-16.
4 Let the testing instruct you, through which you find by how many various oppressions you are exercised, and of how many benefits you are deprived through your disobedience.
5 Hereby he wishes to prove that the person who is deprived of Divine wisdom and saving knowledge cannot be considered happy, even though these people consider it happiness to exercise themselves in the hunting of wild animals, or to gather wealth, or to live in all the pleasures of the flesh. b Isaiah 2:7. c Sirach 5:9.
6 That is: when they say they put their money to work, etc. This refers to those who devise every means and practice to increase their money, and no matter how much they gather, they can never be satisfied, for greed has dominion in their hearts.
7 The Canaanites did not know this wisdom, nor did the Princes of Edom <note>original: "Idamee"</note>; for Teman <note>original: "Thema"</note> is a city situated in the land of the Edomites, on the coastal side of the land of Canaan, where the Princes have their retreat; therefore the people are signified under the name of the city.
8 He calls those who are descended from Ishmael "children of Hagar," because Abraham fathered Ishmael by Hagar his concubine. d Deut. 4:50. Jerem. 23:24. Psalm 103:19.
9 Even though these giants were of great power in the world, also in all physical prowess and boldness, they nevertheless did not obtain wisdom: for it is evident that those who are humbled in themselves are endowed by God with saving knowledge. e Gen. 1:1. Joshua 10:12. Isa. 38:8. Sirach 46:4.
10 Hereby he makes known that the Lord has dominion over all created beings.
</margin>

9 Hear, Israel, the commandments of life; pay diligent attention to them, and keep them well.
10 How is it, Israel, that you languish in the land of the Heathen? That you are in a strange land?
11 That you defile yourself among the dead? That you are counted among those who go down into hell?
12 This is the cause: That you have forsaken the fountain of wisdom.
13 Had you remained in God's ways, you would have lived in peace continually.
14 So learn now right wisdom, so that you may find who it is that gives a long life, goods, and joy.
15 Who knows where she <note>Wisdom is personified as female, following the tradition of "Lady Wisdom."</note> dwells? Who has entered into her chamber?
16 Where are the Princes of the Heathen, who rule over the wild beasts on earth?
17 Who play with the birds of heaven? Who gather silver and gold, in which men set their trust, and can never be satisfied with it?
18 For they gather money and apply themselves to it, and yet it is all in vain.
19 They are rooted out and have gone down into hell, and others have come in their place.
20 The descendants see—it is true—the light indeed, and dwell upon the earth, and yet they do not find the way where one finds <note>original: "bindet" - literally binds or secures.</note> wisdom.
21 For they despised her, and their children have also gone astray.
22 In Canaan, nothing is heard of her; in Teman, she is not seen.
23 The children of Hagar searched—it is true—well after earthly wisdom; likewise the merchants of Meran and those of Teman, who think themselves to be clever: but they do not find the way where one finds wisdom.
24 O Israel, how honorable is the house of the Lord? How wide and great is the place of his dwelling?
25 It has no end, and is immeasurably high.
26 There were in former times giants, their great famous men, and great warriors.
27 The Lord did not choose them, nor did he reveal to them the way of knowledge.
28 And because they had no wisdom, they perished in their foolishness.
29 Who has gone up to heaven and fetched her, and brought her down from the clouds?
30 Who has sailed across the sea and found her, and brought her here for precious gold?
31 In short, there is no one who knows the way where one finds wisdom.
32 But he who knows all things knows her, and has found <note>original: "gebonden" - literally bound.</note> her through his understanding: he who prepared the earth for eternal time, and filled it with all kinds of animals.
33 He who lets the light go forth, and when he calls it back, it must obey him.
34 The stars shine in their order with joy.

### The 5th Chapter.

->1. The Prophet exhorts Jerusalem to joy and gladness because of the deliverance of her people; 4. the name which the Lord shall give to Jerusalem; 7. and 8. the Lord shall be the protector and guide of Israel.<-

<meta>This page transitions between the lament of Jerusalem personified as a grieving mother and the joyful prophecy of the return from the Babylonian exile. It identifies Wisdom as the Torah/Law and interprets the historical return under Cyrus as a precursor to divine salvation.</meta>

<summary>Jerusalem is personified as a widow mourning her children in Babylonian captivity but is soon comforted with the promise of their return. The text emphasizes that their suffering was a result of turning from God's law, and their restoration will be a display of God's eternal glory.</summary>

The text emphasizes that these idols are mere objects made by human hands, susceptible to decay and unable to protect themselves or their worshipers.</summary>

50 Therefore one can from now on recognize that it is a deception, manifest to all Pagans and Kings, and that they are no Gods, but made by human hands, and there is no divinity in them.

12 This becomes manifest through the preaching of the Divine word, which teaches us that it is nothing but vanity. l Isaiah 37:19.
</margin>

51 Therefore every man can well perceive that they are not Gods.

<column-break/>

<margin>
13 Because the works of God are not performed by the Idols, he concludes therefrom that they are not Gods.
</margin>

52 For they do not appoint a King in the land: they do not give rain to mankind.

53 And they take no part in governing or punishing, as little as the birds that fly hither and thither in the air.

54 When the house of the wooden, gilded, and silvered Idols begins to burn with fire, the Priests run away and save themselves from harm: but they [the idols] burn, just like other beams.

55 They can withstand neither Kings nor any soldiers: how then shall they be considered or named as Gods?

56 The wooden, silvered, and gilded idols cannot protect themselves from thieves and robbers: for they are too strong for them, so that they rob them and strip them,

57 Taking away their gold, silver, and clothing, and going off with it: so they cannot help themselves.

<margin>
14 Herewith he also proves their harmful vanity, for the very smallest among any household goods is more useful to men than the mute idols, and yet this is regarded as God; and yet it is written that He is beneficial to all men and harmful to none, just as the Pagans have written in their own books. t Genesis 1:16. u Baruch 3:33.
</margin>

58 Therefore a King who can prove his power, or a useful household tool that is useful in the house, or a door that secures the house, or a wooden pillar in a Royal hall, is much better than such a backwards Idol.

59 The sun, moon, and stars shine, and are obedient in that which God commands them.

60 Likewise the lightning flashes so that one sees it: the wind blows in all lands.

61 And when God commands the clouds to pass over the whole world, they do what God commands them.

62 So also the fire from above strikes the mountains and forests, and does what it is commanded: but the Idols cannot move themselves, nor do anything.

63 Therefore they shall not be considered Gods, or called so: for they can neither punish nor help.

<margin>
x Baruch 6:14, 28.
</margin>

64 Since you then know that they are not Gods, do not fear them.

<margin>
15 That is, they are without any living power, whereby they might do harm or benefit.
</margin>

65 For they can neither curse nor bless Kings.

66 They also cannot show any signs in the heavens to the Pagans: they cannot make light, as the sun does, nor give a reflection like the moon.

67 The irrational animals are better than they: for they can at least run into a shelter and preserve themselves.

68 Therefore it is manifest in every way that they are not Gods.

<margin>
16 Through this parable he makes it known that it is but a ridiculous thing to cling to made idols, and compares them to a scarecrow in the garden, which the birds are at first afraid of, but when they see later that it is nothing but a deception, they may well go and sit on its head.
</margin>

69 For just as a scarecrow <note>Original: *schousel* — a bird-scarer or effigy</note> in the garden cannot protect anything: so also their wooden, gilded, and silvered idols are of no use.

70 And just as a thornbush in the garden, upon which all kinds of birds nest: or just as a dead man who lies in the grave: so are their wooden, gilded, and silvered idols.

71 One can also perceive by this that they are not Gods: for the purple <note>Original: *scharlaken* — though literally "scarlet," in this context it refers to the costly robes of the idols, often translated as purple in biblical texts</note> that they have on is eaten by moths, and they themselves finally as well, so that everyone mocks them.

<margin>
17 That is, he who acts in righteousness, so that he does not rob the living God of His honor.
</margin>

72 Blessed is the man who is righteous and has no Idols: he shall not be put to mockery.

# THE HISTORY OF
## SUSANNA AND DANIEL.

---

<margin>
1 That which is described in this History happened after the first deportation to Babylon, when King Jechonias <note>Also known as Jehoiachin.</note> was led with some of the royal blood into Babylon, among whom Daniel also was; although he was young in years, he was nevertheless gifted with the spirit of wisdom and understanding; thus this occurred eleven years before the destruction of Jerusalem.
2 One cannot know for certain whether this man lived in the city of Babylon or in the surrounding country, as provinces often bore the name of the capital city they were under, just as the land of Babylonia is named after its capital.
3 She was of the tribe of Levi, though many of them were from the tribe of Judah.
a Deut. 6:7.
4 Here, and from other places in Holy Scripture, one can easily notice that the King of Babylon did not live strictly with the people, as he allowed them to choose Superiors and Judges.
5 The Lord spoke this through the mouth of Jeremiah, concerning Zedekiah and Ahab, whom the King of Babylon had roasted by the executioner because of their wickedness: See Jeremiah 29:21-23.
</margin>

<margin>
2. Susanna, Joiakim’s wife. 8. The two elders, namely the Judges, are inflamed with wicked lust for her. 19. They accost her alone in her garden. 20. And she is judged to die. 42. Her prayer. 45. The Lord awakens the spirit of Daniel. 52. The two Elders are defeated by their own mouths. 62. They are put to death.

There was a man in Babylon named Joiakim.
2 He had a wife whose name was Susanna, a daughter of Helkie, who was very beautiful and moreover God-fearing.
3 For she had pious parents who had instructed her according to the Law of Moses.
4 And her husband Joiakim was very rich and had a beautiful garden adjoining his house; and the Jews always gathered at his place, because he was the most prominent man among them all.
5 And in that same year, two elders of the people were appointed as Judges, such men as those of whom the Lord had said: "Their Judges commit all wickedness in Babylon."
6 These same men came daily to Joiakim, <margin>And whoever had a legal case had to appear there before them.</margin> and whoever had a case had to appear there before them.

Judges 10:15 / 12:15.

c Exod. 2:5.
2 Sam. 11:2.
7 Although Susanna was a God-fearing woman, she chose to wash herself in the open where she ought to have been enclosed, if she had need to cleanse her body, so that she might remain hidden from all eyes; she cannot excuse herself by saying she intended to do it secretly, for the history of the matter testifies that her plan failed; she also ought to have considered that even the beauty of some God-fearing women has often been the cause of evil, as with Sarah and Rebecca; furthermore, she ought to have kept before her eyes the example of Bathsheba and David; see then how even the most holy often fall.

# OF BEL IN BABYLON.

1. Daniel is high and great in authority with the King. 2. The Idol of the Babylonians, Bel. 3. The King himself serves and worships him daily. 5. King Cyrus is deceived by the Priests of Bel. 13. The foresight of Daniel in uncovering the falsehood and deceit of the Priests. 19. King Cyrus recognizes their deceit, 21. and they are put to death. 24. Daniel attacks the Dragon. 26. He kills the Dragon. 27. The Babylonians cause a riot against the King. 30. Daniel is cast into the lions' den. 32. The Lord causes food to be carried to him by the Prophet Habakkuk. 33. Daniel is found safe among the lions. 40. The King exalts and magnifies the God of Daniel. 41. The enemies of Daniel are cast into the den and devoured by the lions.

---

<margin>
1 It happened that Astyages, a King of the Medes, gave his only daughter in marriage to a certain Cambyses, a man of very low standing among the Persians, fearing what the soothsayers had told him in the interpretation of his dreams: namely, that his daughter would bear a son who would obtain dominion over all Asia. It happened that she bore a son named Cyrus, whom Astyages commanded to be killed, fearing that he would thrust him out of his kingdom, even though all his friends on his father's side were of low condition. This Cyrus was raised and preserved against the King's command, and having come to his years, and learning that Astyages had wanted to kill him, he took action and drove Astyages out of his kingdom, and delivered the same to the Persians. This happened in the 25th year of King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon, six years after the destruction of Jerusalem.
</margin>

After the death of Astyages, the kingdom came to Cyrus of Persia.

1 ¶ And Daniel was always with the King, and was held in higher honor than all the King’s friends.

2 Now those in Babylon had an idol named Bel, to whom had to be offered daily twelve measures <note>original: "molter," a dry measure roughly equivalent to a bushel</note> of fine flour, and forty sheep, and three jars <note>original: "amen," a liquid measure</note> of wine.

3 And the King himself served the idol and went there daily to pray to it; but Daniel worshipped his own God.

4 And the King said to him: "Why do you not also worship Bel?" He then said: "I do not serve idols made with hands, but the living God, who made heaven and earth and is Lord over everything that lives."

5 Then the King said to him: "Do you not then consider Bel to be a living God? Do you not see how much he eats and drinks?"

6 But Daniel laughed and said: "Lord King, do not be deceived: for this Bel is nothing but clay inside and bronze outside, and has never yet eaten anything."

7 Then the King grew angry and summoned all his Priests, and said to them: "If you do not tell me who consumes these offerings, you shall die."

<column-break/>

<margin>g Leviticus 24:15</margin>
<margin>h Baruch 6:27.</margin>
<margin>
In the entire handling of this history, one might find some difficulty <note>original: "swartcheyt," literally 'blackness' or obscurity</note> regarding the name of the King, seeing as the beginning speaks of Cyrus, and later the idol in Babylon and its priests are mentioned, and finally the sentence of the King over these same "Wise Priests" <note>original: "Wijs Papen," likely a pejorative Reformation-era term for priests</note>. Now, Cyrus did not have jurisdiction in Babylon at that time; therefore, he might not be the one who spoke with the priests about what Daniel had said concerning the idol Bel, and who afterwards had them killed. Instead, it seems more likely this was Nebuchadnezzar, whose name is not explicitly written here. But this discrepancy can easily be reconciled if we consider the friendship that existed between these two Kings: so that Daniel was held in great esteem at both Kings' courts. Therefore, it is reasonable to think that all this business related here was undertaken and lived through by the authority of both Nebuchadnezzar and Cyrus, whom Daniel then advised and assisted.
</margin>

8 "But if you can prove that Bel consumes these things, then Daniel shall die, for he has slandered Bel." And Daniel said: "Yes, Lord King, let it be just as you have spoken."

9 Now there were seventy Priests of Bel, besides their wives and children; and the King went with Daniel into the temple of Bel.

10 Then the Priests said: "Behold, we will go out from here, and you, Lord King, shall set out the food and the wine yourself, and shut the door after you, and seal it with your own ring."

11 "And when you come again early in the morning and find that Bel has not consumed everything, then we will gladly die; otherwise, Daniel shall be put to death, who has lied thus about us."

12 They were confident in this because they had made a secret entrance under the table, and they went in through it all the time and consumed whatever was there.

13 When the Priests had gone out, the King set the food before Bel; but Daniel commanded his servants to fetch ashes, and had them scattered over the entire temple in the presence of the King; then they went out and shut the door, and sealed it with the King’s ring, and departed.

14 Now the Priests went in there by night, according to their custom, with their wives and children, and ate and drank up everything that was there.

15 And very early in the morning, the King arose, and Daniel with him.

16 And the King asked: "Is the seal intact?" He answered: "Yes, Lord King."

17 And as soon as the door was opened, the King looked at the table and cried out with a loud voice: "Bel, you are a great God, and there is no deceit in you."

18 But Daniel laughed and held the King back so that he would not go inside, and said: "Look at the floor, and notice whose footprints these are?"

19 The King said: "I see indeed the footprints of men, women, and children." Then the King became angry.

20 And he had the Priests seized, along with their wives and children; and they had to show him the secret passages through which they had gone in and out to consume what was on the table.

21 And the King had them put to death, and gave Bel into Daniel’s power; who then destroyed him and his temple.

# A very useful Chart / serving for the knowledge of the Jewish state / and begins from the reign of the Greeks / (at which the Chart that we have added to the Book of Ezra / ends /) until the death and the suffering of Jesus Christ.

->**The seventy weeks prophesied by Dan. 9.**<-

---

The Angel of the Lord sent to Daniel informed him that there would be 70 year-weeks / that is to say / seventy times seven / which makes 490 years / according to the word that was spoken / that Jerusalem should be rebuilt / and established until Christ the Leader and Prince. Which word was spoken through the mouth of Darius Longimanus <note>Darius Longimanus is likely a reference to Artaxerxes I Longimanus, whose 20th year is cited in Nehemiah 2 as the start of the rebuilding.</note> of the Persians, Monarch in the 20th year of his reign / just as it stands written in Nehemiah 2. Therefore, one ought to count the 70 weeks from that time / although all Authors do not agree on this: for some begin at the 2nd year of the aforementioned Darius. Others at the first year of Cyrus. Thus, from the beginning of the aforementioned weeks / until the time that Alexander took up the Monarchy / one counts 18 weeks and 4 years / making 130 years. And to truly prove these aforementioned weeks / following the preceding prophecy of Daniel 9, we shall measure them against the years in which the Kings of Syria (marked below on the right side) have governed their kingdom: each of them one against the other.

->**The Monarchy of the Greeks.**<-

---

Alexander the Great / son of Philip / King of Macedonia / conquered the Monarchy of Persia from Darius / in the hundred and ninety-second year of Cyrus / the first ruler / and transported <note>Meaning he transferred the seat of power or culture.</note> the Greeks. He reigned six full years / and died in the seventh / leaving many <unclear>descendants</unclear> behind / to whom he divided his aforementioned reign (before his death): namely / the Kingdoms of Syria / Asia / Egypt / and Macedonia. We shall here only treat of his successors / who were Kings of Syria / because the Scripture speaks of them / and makes its counting / with the years that the aforementioned Kings reigned / beginning with the first / as one sees in the first Book of the Maccabees. And we shall set their names in order / with also the time that each reigned / to set and compare them against the number that stands on the left side of this chart: in order thus to truly prove the seventy weeks / and to better understand the prophecy (written in Daniel / concerning the coming of Jesus Christ).

2 Antiochus Soter possessed the kingdom of Syria / eleven years / and reigned nineteen years. <margin>50</margin>
3 Antiochus Theos began his reign in the 51st year / and reigned fifteen years. <margin>65</margin>

# THE FIRST BOOK 
## OF THE MACCABEES.

### Short Summary of this Book.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring a scholar or biblical figure seated and holding a book, surrounded by architectural motifs.</image-desc>
Since human beings are by nature so inclined that they very quickly grow sluggish in times of earthly peace and prosperity, and become sleepy in matters that serve the honor of God and His glory—which is undoubtedly a perilous and deadly harm—the Lord therefore provides a safeguard (much like a faithful physician who loves his patients and his chosen ones and does not wish for them to perish). He administers a very fitting medicine, even though it is contrary to the flesh and the "old man" <note>A theological term referring to the unregenerate human nature.</note>: namely, that He continually tests and exercises His church and the faithful through various trials and persecutions. This is so that, being pricked, they may wake up and know how to conduct themselves properly in their calling. Scripture demonstrates this to us figuratively in Isaac and Ishmael, in Jacob and Esau, and in truth and deed within the ancient people who were the church of God. ¶ For we see what state the Israelites were in while in Egypt; what wars they had to withstand in the land of Canaan against many kinds of enemies; how they were also led away as captives into Assyria on one side and Babylon on the other; and after returning to their land, how they were attacked, persecuted, and distressed, partly by their neighbors and partly by tyrants and kings. This history in the first book of the Maccabees sets this fully before us and places it visibly before our eyes. And just as we must observe the very great and heavy persecutions and anxieties of this people herein, so we must also, on the other hand, behold the wonderful and powerful works of God, as He with His strong hand and outstretched arm mightily delivered this people from their sorrow. This must serve as a certain comfort to us in our adversity, as we are taught by such examples that the Lord will likewise come to our aid in our need (even if He delays for a time) and will deliver us when we least hope for it and know no further counsel—just as He always faithfully and in deed proved to His church and people in Egypt, in the land of Canaan, in Assyria, and in Babylon, seeing as He brought them back and restored them to their land. Now, this history also tends toward the end that it wishes to teach and show us the same thing, while it places before our eyes the state of God's people as being very desolate and torn apart by the organized wantonness and tyranny of the enemies—indeed, in all matters appearing as if hopeless and lost. For the capital city had fallen into the hands of the enemies, the temple was defiled with idolatry, the holy vessels were stolen, the people were scattered and slaughtered; those who had escaped the sword fled into the deserts, or they forsook the law and their religion. In short, nothing remained but to say: it is over and done with. But the Lord, after all hope had failed, then worked according to His custom, so that no flesh should boast before Him and that all honor should come to Him alone; for He raised up Mattathias with his sons as an instrument of His work, performing wonderful things through them. He destroyed the great pride and power of the enemies and fully restored the state of His church, making the name of His people highly esteemed and also feared and respected by all other nations, as all this is abundantly described in this book. Furthermore, it is to be noted that Mattathias and his sons are called the Maccabees because of Judas the Maccabee, who was appointed as a head and Prince, the first from the priestly lineage of the <term>Hasmoneans</term> <note>original: "Asmoneers"</note>, named after one Asmoneus from whom they descended. Also, these Maccabees joined and concluded in their lineage and persons both the royal power and the priestly dignity, although they did not claim the title of King for themselves until Aristobulus, who was a son of John Hyrcanus, who was a son of Simon the Maccabee. This Aristobulus placed the royal crown on his head and also bore the title. The author of this book is unknown; nevertheless, its content is holy and very useful, which is why it has been accepted and admitted into the church of the Lord.

After him came to the kingdom Antiochus Soter, King in Asia and Syria, who reigned 19 years. The third was Antiochus Theos, who sat in the kingdom 15 years. The fourth was Seleucus Gallinicus, 20 years. The fifth, Seleucus Ceraunus, 3 years. The sixth, Antiochus the Great, 36 years. The seventh, Seleucus Philopator, 11 years, a son of the aforementioned Antiochus the Great. The eighth, Antiochus Epiphanes, of whom is spoken here, a son of the aforementioned Antiochus and a brother of Seleucus. This one was sent by his father as a hostage or pledge-man to Rome, and having returned, he took the Kingdom from his brother and reigned 12 years. All the years of this book, from the first until the beginning of this Antiochus the Noble, amount to 137 years in total.

### The 4th Chapter.

i. The army of Gorgias is defeated by Judas Maccabeus; 22. Gorgias, defeated, flees; 23. Judas plunders the camp of the enemies; 24. The Jews sing songs of praise to the Lord and thank Him; 28. 1 And Gorgias took five thousand footmen and a thousand of the best horsemen, and set out by night secretly toward the Jews' camp to fall upon them unawares.
2 And some who lay in the garrison at the citadel <note>The "citadel" refers to the Acra, a fortress in Jerusalem occupied by Seleucid forces and pro-Greek Jews.</note> acted as guides for the group.
3 But Judas was up beforehand with his best men, so that he might arrive first and surprise the enemies.
4 And he struck them while they still lay scattered here and there.
5 Now when Gorgias came to Judas's camp and found no one there, he pursued them into the mountains, thinking they had fled from him.
6 But Judas hurried so that he came into the field early in the morning with three thousand men, who nevertheless had no armor, but only their clothes and swords.

Now when the Heathens round about heard that the Altar was rebuilt and the sanctuary restored, they were very angry.
<margin>1 This was a city located between Idumea and Arabia, named Petrea <note>original: "Petrea, dat is/ steenich"</note>, which means "stony": they began to cause trouble at the time Antiochus began to attack them; they took flight into Idumea, fearing they might fall into his hands. And now that Judas has brought all things back into good order, the Idumeans being inflamed with great hatred, have sworn to persecute those who had fled to them; therefore Judas now wants to come to their aid.</margin>
2 And they determined to wipe out the whole generation of Jacob, and began to kill all the Jews within their borders.
<margin>2 Which being enclosed from before, dwelt near the Idumeans and Ammonites. Thus also the scripture speaks of the children of Ammon and the children of Esau: and the ancients call them the Eastern Idumeans.</margin>
3 But Judas marched into Idumea against the children of Esau, and fell upon them at Akrabattene <note>original: "Arabath"</note>, where they had besieged the children of Israel, and he struck many Idumeans dead and plundered them.

<margin>18 Mount Zion was higher than Mount Moriah, which lay next to it on the same side. Now, the Temple was built on Mount Moriah and not on Zion; nevertheless, it says here that they went up to Zion and offered sacrifices there, etc. Therefore, Zion is used here to refer to Moriah because of their proximity, and because these two mountains are joined together. Or it may be understood that Zion signifies the entire mountain, and Moriah is just the part of the mountain where the Temple stood. Just as Lebanon is used generally for the entire mountain range located on the north side of the Jewish land, yet it is often used to refer to a specific part of Mount Lebanon. One part is called Hermon, another part Anti-Lebanon, and on the eastern side, a part is called Gilead.</margin>

### The VII. Chapter.

> *i. 1 In the one hundred and fifty-first year, Demetrius the son of Seleucus came from Rome back into his Kingdom, and took a city by the sea with a few people: and reigned there as a King.

2 And when he came into the capital city, Antioch, the soldiers seized Antiochus and Lysias to deliver them to Demetrius.

3 When this was told to Demetrius, he commanded that they should not be allowed to come before his eyes: therefore the soldiers killed them.

<margin>
**1** This Demetrius was a son of Seleucus, who was a son of Antiochus the Great, and also a brother of Antiochus Epiphanes the tyrant. Thus the aforementioned Antiochus took the Kingdom, which by right should have belonged to Demetrius as the true heir of his father Seleucus, who was an older brother of Antiochus. Now while this Demetrius was in Rome as a hostage or guarantor, he heard that his uncle Antiochus Epiphanes (or the noble) had died; he came to Syria, where he was welcome and received the crown, but after reigning eight years, he was killed.
</margin>

4 Now when Demetrius held the kingdom, many godless and apostate people from Israel came to him: and the most prominent among them was Alcimus, who dearly wished to have become high priest.

5 These accused Judas and their own people, saying: Judas and his brothers have killed all those who wanted to be obedient to you, or have chased them out of our land.

6 Therefore send someone there whom you trust, and let him see it, and take the Kingdom out of the hands of the arrogance of the young King, of whom we spoke above, who was killed after reigning eight years. <note>2</note> This man had changed his name which he previously bore, namely Joakim, into this heathen name.

45 Then the people ran out from all the villages round about the land to pursue them, and they helped to strike down the enemies: and they came toward Judah and turned back against them: so the army of Nicanor was struck down, and not one of them escaped.

### The 8th Chapter.

->*1. Judas sends to the Romans for a treaty; 27. Eupolemus and Jason, ambassadors, arrive in Rome; 21. and 22. they are well received by the Council; 23. the conditions of peace and fellowship between the Jews and the Romans.*<-

<margin>
Chapter 8.
a Josephus, Antiquities, Book 12, Chapter 7.
1 Note: Against the Galatians. These had once had a tribute imposed on them by the Romans, but this was more as a sign of the dominion they held over them than because they were greedy for money. It is also more credible that the Galatians are spoken of here than the Gauls, who at that time had not yet been brought under Roman power.
</margin>
1 Now Judas heard that the Romans were very powerful and gladly took foreign peoples under their protection who sought help from them: and that they kept faith and loyalty.

2 For he heard what honorable deeds they had done against the Gauls, <gloss>n.1.</gloss> whom they had subdued and brought under their control.

<margin>
2 The Roman wars fought in Spain, both against the Carthaginians (who held a great part of the land) and against various other peoples of that same land whom they overcame, are very famous and magnificently described by the Latin and Greek historians.
</margin>
3 Also what great wars they <gloss>n.2.</gloss> had waged in Spain, and had taken the mines where gold and silver are dug.

<margin>
3 They brought many distant nations, located even as far as the Parthians, under their power, along with the kings of those same lands; see under verse 8.
</margin>
4 And that they had won many lands, <gloss>n.3.</gloss> far from Rome, with great ingenuity and earnestness, and held them: that they also had struck down and driven away many powerful kings who had marched into their land, and brought their kingdoms under them.

<margin>
4 This Philip was a king in Macedonia and one of the last to reign there. Perseus, against whom the Romans sent a consul, Paulus Aemilius, with a great army, also defeated the aforementioned Perseus and brought the entire land and kingdom of Macedonia under the subjection of the Roman people. These Macedonians are here called Kittim. b 1 Maccabees 1:1.
</margin>
5 And that they <gloss>n.4.</gloss> had recently overcome the king of Kittim, Philip, and afterward his son Perseus.

<margin>
5 This is the reason why Antiochus Epiphanes’ son was sent as a hostage, and after him Demetrius, as is recounted in this history.
</margin>
6 Also of the great <gloss>n.5.</gloss> Antiochus, the king in Asia, who had marched against the Romans with a hundred and twenty elephants, with a great cavalry force and chariots: but the Romans had defeated his army and forced him to plead for peace.

7 And they had imposed on him, and his successors after him, a great tribute which they had to give to the Romans annually: furthermore, he had to send hostages to the Romans.

<margin>
6 Namely: they stripped King Antiochus of many lands and lordships, which they then redistributed.
</margin>
8 They took <gloss>n.6.</gloss> from him also Ionia, Asia, and Lydia, the noblest lands, and gave them to King Eumenes.

<margin>
7 Pyrrhus, King of the Epirotes, waged a great war against the Romans, and that for no other reason than that he wanted to bring them under his subjection and seize their empire. He crossed over into Italy and achieved fair and many victories against the aforementioned Romans, but at last he was forced to depart, being overcome by a consul and commander named Fabricius.
</margin>
9 Also the Greeks set themselves <gloss>n.7.</gloss> with

<column-break/>

great power against them.

10 But they sent a commander against the Greeks, who defeated them and took the land, and had the walls of the cities torn down, so that they had to keep peace and be obedient.

11 Such earnestness they showed against all their enemies, that they subdued all those who set themselves against them.

12 But with their friends and allies they kept good peace and held faith, and were powerful, and were respected in all lands.

13 Whomever they helped was protected and kept in his kingdom: but whomever they wished to punish was driven out from land and people.

14 And there was such virtue among them that no one made himself king.

15 And they also had no king, but a Council, which was three hundred and twenty men, who governed well.

<margin>
8 The Roman government was not a monarchy, but the supreme height and principal authority belonged to all the common people, who annually chose two consuls, so that they, along with the council (which at that time consisted of 320 men), would govern the commonwealth, as is recounted in the following verse.
9 The two consuls did not rule simultaneously, but each his own power in turn: and therefore it is said here that one leader was chosen annually. b 1 Maccabees 12:1, 15:17. 2 Maccabees 4:11.
</margin>
16 And annually they chose <gloss>n.8.</gloss> a leader <note>original: "hooftman" - referring to the Roman Consuls</note>, who had command in all their lands: to him they all had to be obedient: and there was no pride, envy, or discord among them.

17 ¶ And Judas chose <gloss>n.9.</gloss> Eupolemus the son of John, the son of Jacob, and Jason, Eleazar's son, and sent them to Rome to make friendship and a treaty with the Romans.

<margin>
10 Meaning: So that the Kingdom of the Greeks would not oppress Israel. After the death of Alexander the Great, all the kingdoms that were established were called by the name of the Greek Kingdom. See above chapter 1:1. But the kingdom spoken of here is Demetrius’s kingdom, namely, of Syria and Asia.
</margin>
18 So that they might help them, <gloss>n.10.</gloss> that the Kingdom of Israel would not be oppressed by the Greeks.

19 These traveled to Rome, a long way, and came before the Council and spoke thus:

20 Judas Maccabeus and his brothers, and the Jewish people, have sent us to you to make a peace and treaty with you, that you would take us under your protection as friends and allies.

21 This pleased the Romans well.

22 And they had that treaty written on bronze tablets, which they sent to Jerusalem as a memorial of the peace and treaty made: and it read thus:

23 May God give the Romans and Jews success and peace, by land and by water, and protect them from war and enemies forever.

24 However, if the Romans shall have war to come, either in their lands or territories,

25 Then the Jews shall faithfully give help to the Romans, as the necessity requires.

<margin>
11 The Lord has always remembered his people and also punished them in deed whenever they made alliances with foreign nations for their fortification. Namely: with the Egyptians or Assyrians; and that because it sufficiently showed and declared that they did not trust the Lord and His promises, which is a species of idolatry and mistrust. Now Judas Maccabeus, although he was a very virtuous and God-fearing man, nevertheless falls into this sin, making a treaty with the Romans, for which in the end it also goes poorly for him. For he does not reign long after this and is also overcome by those whom he himself had so often defeated.
</margin>
26 And they shall not send to the Romans' enemies any food, weapons, money, ships, or other things: this the Romans desire of the Jews: and they shall <unclear>faithfully</unclear> keep such terms, without any deceit or craftiness.

27 Conversely, also, if the Jews shall have war, the Romans shall faithfully help them, as the necessity requires.

28 And they shall not send to the Jews' enemies any food, weapons, money, ships, or other things: this the Romans promise, and they will keep such a treaty faithfully and without deceit.

29 Thus the treaty between the Romans and Jews was made.

### The 9th Chapter.
