<margin>
Chap. 9.
a Josephus, Antiquities, Book 12, Chapter 17. 1 Maccabees 7:7, 8.
1 See Deuteronomy 1:39 and Joshua 5:9. Arbela is the end of the outermost borders of the land of Judah, toward the East; at that same place was also the city called here Masloth.
2 This matter must be counted beginning as it is related above in chapter 1:11.
3 This anxiety proves the same thing that was said here previously in the preceding chapter regarding the covenant he had established with the Romans: namely, that Judas did not have a certain and steadfast faith, seeing as he relied on the "arm of the flesh," <note>a biblical idiom meaning relying on human strength rather than God</note> for which reason it ultimately went poorly for him.
4 Previously, when Judas fought with a small band of people against Apollonius and the great army of King Antiochus, he called upon the name and help of the Lord, and confessed as much with his heart as with his mouth, that it is easy for the Lord to deliver many people into the hands of the few, and that it makes no difference at all to the God of heaven to save his people with a great number or with a tiny small band; therefore, with few people, he often laid low a great army. But now, since he pursues other purposes and no longer speaks boldly in the name of the Lord—and forgets to call upon the Lord's name in a spirit of pride—the Lord also pays him back, so that victory does not consist in the boldness of the heart.
</margin>
1 **I**n the meantime, when Demetrius heard that Nicanor and his army had been defeated and had perished, he sent these two, Bacchides and Alcimus, back into Judea, and with them his very best soldiers, who were accustomed to stand on the right wing in battles.
2 These marched toward Galgala and besieged and captured Masloth in Arbela, and killed many people there.
3 Afterward, in the one hundred and fifty-second year, in the first month, they marched toward Jerusalem.
4 And from there to Berea, with twenty thousand footmen and two thousand horsemen.
5 And Judas camped by Laisa with three thousand men.
6 But when his people saw that the enemies had such a great power, they were terrified and fled from there; so that no more remained with Judah than eight hundred men.
7 When Judas saw this, that his army did not stay together, and yet the enemies pressed upon him, he became anxious; and when he saw that he had no space to comfort his people and bring them back together,
8 He spoke in this distress to those who remained: "Arise, and let us try if we can attack the enemies and defeat them."
9 But they would not, and discouraged him, saying: "It is not possible for us to accomplish anything; but let us withdraw for this time and retreat, and bring back our brothers who have run from us; then we will go back against the enemies and attack them; for now we are far too few."
10 But Judas said: "Far be it from us that we should flee: if our time has come, then we will die gallantly for our brothers' sake, and not let our honor be put to shame."

<column-break/>

11 And the enemies were up and prepared their battle order thus: The first were the archers, and the best warriors stood at the front of the spearhead; the horsemen were divided into two groups, one on each side.
12 The captain Bacchides was on the right side. With this order, they marched there with great shouting and the sounding of trumpets.
13 Then Judas also had the trumpets sounded and marched against them, and he fought a battle with them from the morning until the evening, so that the earth trembled from the great noise.
14 When Judas now saw that Bacchides himself was on the right side with the greatest part of the power, he attacked there, he and the others who risked their lives:
15 And they terrified them and drove that same group on the right side into flight, and chased them as far as Mount 
<margin>§ See regarding Azotus above in chapter 4:13.</margin>
Azotus.
16 Now when those on the left side saw that Judas was chasing some away, they also chased after Judah; then Judas had to turn against these and defended himself for a long time.
17 And there occurred a hard slaughter, so that many were wounded there and perished on both sides,
18 Until Judas also finally perished: then those who remained fled.
19 And Jonathan and Simon took the body of their brother Judas and buried him in the tomb of his fathers.
20 And all the people of Israel mourned for Judas for a long time: and they lamented him greatly, saying:
21 "Oh, that the hero has perished, who protected and liberated Israel!"
<margin>
b Josephus, Antiquities, book 13, Chapter 1.
6 All the Jews who had fallen away from their religion—those who knew that Judas still lived and also those who had followed him through pretense and hypocrisy—betook themselves to Alcimus, who had been ordained as high priest by King Demetrius. And Alcimus brought them all together under his yoke, so that they should live according to the works and ordinances of King Demetrius. This Jonathan was the brother of Judas the Maccabee; see above, chapter 2, verse 5.
8 When Jonathan was still without command or rule, no one persecuted him; but now that he is exalted in authority and power, he is attacked by his enemies with worries, trouble, and anxiety. Thus it generally goes for those who are burdened and commissioned with great and heavy affairs in public matters.
</margin>
22 This is the history of Judah: but he has done many other great deeds besides, which, because of their great number, are not all written down.
23 After the death of Judah, the godless and apostate people became powerful again in the whole land of Israel.
24 And at this time there was a great famine in the land, so that the whole people surrendered themselves to Bacchides.
25 Then Bacchides chose godless men and made them into officials.
26 And he had Judas’s followers and friends sought out everywhere and brought before him, so that he might take revenge on them and exercise his wantonness upon them.
27 And there was such sorrow and misery in Israel, the likes of which had not been since the time when there were no Prophets.
28 Therefore Judas’s followers came together and spoke to Jonathan:
29 "Since your brother’s death, we have no one else like him to protect us against our enemies and Bacchides, who persecutes us.
30 Therefore we choose you in his place to be a prince and captain, to lead this war."
31 Thus Jonathan became their prince and ruled in his brother's place.
32 When Bacchides became aware of this, he had him sought out so that he might kill him.

### The 10th Chapter.

<margin>Chapter 10.</margin>
<margin>1 Alexander, the son of Antiochus the Noble, reigns in Ptolemais; 3 and 15 Demetrius and Alexander both desire friendship with Jonathan; 18 Alexander’s letter to Jonathan; 46 Jonathan accepts Alexander’s friendship; 49 Demetrius is defeated in battle by Alexander; 51 Alexander makes an alliance with Ptolemy, the King of Egypt, and marries his daughter; 60 Jonathan is honorably received by Alexander; 69 Apollonius is sent by Demetrius into Judea to harass them; 78 he is defeated in battle by Jonathan and his brother Simon; 84 the city of Ashdod is burned with the temple of Dagon by Jonathan.</margin>
<margin>1 This chronology begins with the start of the Kingdom <note>The text says "of Spain," which is likely an OCR error or an early modern geographical confusion for "Syria" or the Seleucid Era</note> after the death of Alexander the Great; see above chapter 1:11.
2 This Antiochus was the Tyrant who was discussed in the beginning of this book. Regarding Ptolemais, you may see above chapter 5:15.
Furthermore, the historian writes that this Alexander, the son of Antiochus, was not his true son, but rather a "changeling" <note>A common early modern term for a child substituted for another; the historian implies Alexander Balas was an impostor</note> of low birth named Balas <note>OCR reads "Propatus," likely a corruption of "Balas"</note>; and that the Kings of Egypt, Asia, and Cappadocia, who were all enemies of Demetrius, urged him to reclaim the Kingdom of Syria by legal succession (since he pretended that Antiochus was his father). So he set out with help from the aforementioned kings, and also from the Syrians who hated Demetrius, so that he defeated Demetrius and brought the Kingdom under his subjection. 1 Maccabees 9:53.</margin>
1 In the one hundred and sixtieth year, Alexander, the son of Antiochus * the Noble <note>original: "des Edelen," referring to Antiochus IV Epiphanes</note>, arrived and took the city of Ptolemais, and reigned there.
2 When Demetrius heard of this, he gathered a great army and marched against Alexander to drive him out.
3 Therefore Demetrius wrote to Jonathan and promised him: He wished to keep peace with him and do him every kindness.
4 For he thought: It is better that I bring him to my side first, before he joins with Alexander against me.
5 Especially since I have killed his brother and done much harm to him and his people.
6 And Demetrius wrote to Jonathan and promised him that he could recruit and maintain soldiers and prepare armaments, and that he should be his ally; and he commanded that the hostages in the citadel should be released to Jonathan.
7 Therefore Jonathan came to Jerusalem and had these letters read before all the people and before those who were in the citadel.
<margin>3 This fear was among the apostate Jews, who feared that Jonathan would take revenge for their unfaithfulness.</margin>
8 When they heard that the King allowed him to recruit soldiers and that the King considered him an ally, they were greatly afraid of him.
9 And they released the hostages to him, and Jonathan gave them back to their parents.
10 Thus Jonathan began to live in Jerusalem, and to rebuild and improve the city.
11 And he had the walls rebuilt and Mount Zion fortified again with good, strong walls of solid hewn stone; thus Jerusalem was built strong again.
12 And the heathens, in the strongholds that Bacchides had fortified,
13 Fled away from there into their own land.
<margin>4 The heathens who were stationed as garrisons throughout the whole land left their strongholds, but in Beth-zur remained the Jews who had sided with the heathens. See regarding Beth-zur chapter 4:61.</margin>
14 Only Beth-zur they kept, and the apostates fled there: for that was where they had their maintenance.
15 When Alexander learned that Demetrius sought friendship with Jonathan, and heard of the praiseworthy deeds that Jonathan and his brothers had done,

18 King Alexander sends greetings to his

brother Jonathan.

20 Therefore we appoint you as High Priest over your people, and you shall be called the King’s friend; and we send you herewith a purple robe and a golden crown: so that you may hold faithfully to us and remain our friend.
<margin>5 This was the month we call September; for the calculation of years see above chap. 1:11 and Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book 13, chapter 3.</margin>

23 That Alexander had turned the Jews away from him to himself, and thereby became stronger.

<margin>6 He speaks of the debt he expected to receive from them, because they were behind a certain time in the payment of tributes. 30 From these burdens, the land of Judah and the three districts belonging to it in the lands of Samaria and Galilee shall henceforth be free forever.
31 And Jerusalem shall be holy and free from all burdens, tribute, and tithes.
32 I will also have the citadel at Jerusalem cleared and give it to the High Priest, so that he may occupy it and place people there whom he wishes to guard it.
33 And all imprisoned Jews in my Kingdom shall be released and set free; and they and their cattle shall be exempt from taxes.
34 They shall also have the freedom throughout my Kingdom to observe their Sabbaths, New Moons, and other appointed feasts.
35 And for three days before and after the feasts, no man shall hinder them in their worship of God.
36 And thirty thousand men shall be chosen in Judea to whom I will give wages, just as to my other soldiers, and they shall be stationed in the King’s fortified cities.
37 And some shall be chosen from them whom the King will use in his greatest affairs as trusted advisors; the Jews shall also have no foreign leaders, but their own chosen from among them, so that they may keep their law just as in the land of Judah.
<margin>8 In the region of Samaria, located between Judea and Galilee, were three districts that were formerly administered separately. Demetrius now joins all these together with the Jewish land.</margin>
38 And the three districts in the land of Samaria and Galilee that belong to Judea shall be subject to no one but the High Priest alone: so that it may be known that he alone is Lord over them.

### The 11th Chapter.

<margin>Chap. xi.</margin>

1 <margin>a Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews, book 13, chapter 7.</margin> And the King of Egypt gathered an army as numerous as the sand on the seashore, and many ships, seeking to seize Alexander’s kingdom for himself through deceit, so that he might rule both kingdoms.

cities opened to him and the people came to meet him and received him honorably, as Alexander had commanded, since he was the father of the King's wife.

### The 16th Chapter.

> 1. Simon sends his two sons against Cendebeus, 6. the bravery of John, the son of Simon, 8. Cendebeus is put to flight and his army scattered, 11. Ptolemy the son of Abubus, 15. the treachery of Ptolemy against Simon and his children.

# The First Book of the Maccabees.

<margin>
Chapter 16.
a. Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book 13, Chapter 12. 1 Maccabees 13:54.
1. This was John Hyrcanus, the son [of Simon], who was named Hyrcanus because he had brought those of Hyrcania under his rule. <note>John Hyrcanus I was a high priest and prince of the Hasmonean Dynasty who significantly expanded the Judean state.</note>
</margin>

1 Then John went up from Gaza to his father Simon and reported to him that Cendebeus had invaded the land and had caused great damage.
2 Then Simon summoned his two eldest sons, Judas and John, and spoke to them: "I and my brothers, and my father’s house, have waged war from our youth until this day against the enemies of the people of Israel; and God has given us such success that Israel has often been delivered by our hands.
3 But since I am now old and weak, you shall step into my place and the place of my brothers; go out and fight for your people. May God from Heaven help you and be with you."
4 And he chose out of the country twenty thousand men and some horsemen; with this host, John and Judas marched against Cendebeus and stayed the night at ² Modin.

<margin>
2. Modin was a city of Judah from which the Maccabees originated: see above, Chapter 2, verse 1.
3. The Lord had commanded His people to use trumpets in war, which the Levites kept in their care; they blew them to make known to the people the good will of the Lord, and that He was ready to help them. And when the enemies heard the blowing of the trumpets, they were so terrified that they could not stand before the people of God, just as the power of these same trumpets is seen here in John’s army.
</margin>

5 Now in the morning, when they came from Modin into the open plain, a great host of footmen and horsemen marched against them; however, there was a stream between the two armies.
6 Then John moved toward the stream and turned to face the enemy; but when he saw that the people were afraid to cross into the water, he himself waded in first and crossed the water. When the host saw this, they followed after him.
7 Then John drew up his battle lines and stationed the horsemen among the footmen; but the enemy had a much more powerful force of horsemen.
8 When John ³ ordered the trumpets to be sounded, along with the priests' trumpets, and attacked the enemy, Cendebeus fled with his army, and many were wounded and pierced through; those who remained fled into a ⁴ fortified settlement.
9 In this battle, Judas, John’s brother, was also wounded; but John pursued the enemy ⁵ as far as the fortress of Cedron.

<margin>
4. This was the settlement of Cedron, which had been fortified: see above, Chapter 15:40.
b. 1 Maccabees 15:41.
5. The meaning of this verse is that John pursued the enemy into the towers they had built in the settlement of Azotus <note>Original: "Azod"</note> for their fortification; and by burning these towers, he slew about two thousand men, after which victory he returned again to Jerusalem in peace.
</margin>

10 And the enemy fled to the fortress in the land near Azotus; then John burned that same fortress, so that about two thousand of the enemy perished. Afterward, John returned home to the land of Judah in peace.
11 And there was a captain over the region of Jericho named Ptolemy, the son of Abubus, who was very wealthy.
12 And the High Priest Simon had given him a daughter [in marriage].
13 Therefore he was proud and aspired

<column-break/>

to become a lord in the land, and he sought to do away with Simon and his sons through treachery.

g. 2 Samuel 13:28.

</margin>

14 Now while Simon was traveling through the land of Judah to inspect and arrange the governance, he came to Jericho with two of his sons, Mattathias and Judas, in the one hundred and seventy-seventh year, in the eleventh month, which is called Shebat.

<margin>
7. This was Antiochus who was spoken of in Chapter 15, verse 1. <note>Antiochus VII Sidetes.</note>
c. 2 Maccabees 14:1.

15 Then the son of Abubus received them at his castle, which is called Dok, and prepared a magnificent feast for them; but it was pure deception, for he had secretly hidden soldiers there.
16 ⁶ And when Simon and his sons were merry ⁷ and had drunk well, Ptolemy rose up with his servants and took their weapons; they fell upon Simon where they sat and struck him dead, along with his two sons and servants.
17 This shameful betrayal Ptolemy committed in Israel, and he repaid such evil for the kindness shown to him.
18 Afterward, he wrote of these things to King Antiochus and prayed that he would send soldiers to help him take over the land, the cities, and all that belonged to them.
19 He also sent a group to Gaza to kill John, and wrote to the captains that they should come to him, promising them great wages and gifts.
20 He also dispatched soldiers to take Jerusalem and the sanctuary.
21 But a messenger reached Gaza first and told John that his father and his brothers had perished, and that it was ordered that he should also be killed.
22 When John heard this, he was greatly dismayed; he had the men seized who had been sent to kill him, and when he learned that they intended to murder him, he had them put to death.

<margin>
8. This John served in both the priestly and princely office for thirty-one years and did many honorable things for the welfare of his people. After his death, his son Aristobulus reigned for only one year and received the royal crown in the year 484 after the exile to Babylon. He killed his mother and brothers. After him came Alexander Jannaeus, a cruel tyrant; and when he was about to die, he handed the kingdom over to the hands of Alexandra, his wife, despite the fact that he left two children behind, namely, Hyrcanus and Aristobulus. This Alexandra reigned for nine years and had her son Hyrcanus serve the priestly office because he could not hold both offices. After her death, Hyrcanus reigned for three months and was driven out by his brother Aristobulus, who robbed him of both the priestly and royal offices and reigned in his place for about three years and seven months. And while these two brothers fought against each other for the high office, Pompey, as head of the Roman army, took it from both of them and brought the entire land of the Jews under obedience [to Rome].
</margin>

23 As for the rest of what John did afterward, ⁸ and the wars he waged, and how he ruled and built,
24 These are all written in a special book of the time of his reign, as long as he was High Priest after his father.

->End of the First Book of the<-
->Maccabees.<-

---

[The narrative concludes with the] cooperation of the Romans, leaving Hyrcanus in the priestly office, while the other brother, Aristobulus, was taken away as a prisoner. They appointed Antipater, the father of Herod, over the administration of the Jewish land; and twenty-two years later, the Roman authorities ordained Herod to be a King of the Jewish land, who took the scepter from Judah just as Christ came into the world.

<summary>This final chapter details the victory of John Hyrcanus over Cendebeus and the subsequent assassination of the High Priest Simon and his sons by his son-in-law Ptolemy. It concludes by noting John's succession and the eventual transition of Judea into a Roman client state under Herod.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the end of 1 Maccabees to the beginning of 2 Maccabees. The previous page concluded the history of Simon and the rise of John Hyrcanus. This page serves as a critical introduction to the second book, highlighting its status as Apocrypha and its historical discrepancies compared to the first book.</meta>

# THE SECOND BOOK
## OF THE MACCABEES.

->Short contents of this Book.<-

Inasmuch as the Spirit of God well knew how weak we are by nature, and how unfit we would be to understand his teachings if he were to speak to us in such a manner as would befit his Majesty, he has, seeing our weakness, not refused to babble with us just as a wet-nurse does with a young child. Yet within this, such a glory, majesty, and working power are seen that it penetrates to the innermost parts of the heart, which he has softened from all stubbornness. And this reveals itself as well in the Apocrypha as in the other books of Holy Scripture, except for this second book of the Maccabees, which, as many learned men testify, might well be left aside by the church without any harm. For besides the fact that the honest and powerful style of the Spirit is not found herein, there are many strange arguments in it that strive against the Holy Scripture, such as when he speaks of the number of those whom Judas Maccabeus killed, which contradicts what is written in the first book of the Maccabees, as one shall find when comparing one against the other. Likewise, of the Angel on horseback, and two youths with him; of the horse-mounted cavalry with gilded spears, who were seen in the air for forty days, and that for the sake of the prayer that Onias the High Priest made; of the fire which was placed in a deep pit before the captivity of Babylon, and which was supposedly found after the deliverance of Nehemiah, of which neither Ezra nor Nehemiah mention a single word. And more other similar things, which the Rabbis and Doctors of the Jews may have composed according to their custom, and thereafter placed in the History of Jason of Cyrene, from which this book is taken as a short summary. Likewise is also that which is written herein concerning the offerings and prayers for the forgiveness of sins for the dead: <note>The translator is warning the reader about the theological implications of 2 Maccabees 12:43-45, which was used to support the doctrine of Purgatory.</note> besides that this horrible abuse is greatly strengthened to the trampling of the blood of Christ, not only through the greed of the Jews, but also of those who wish to boast of the name of Christ in vain. All this considered, everyone shall read this book with upright judgment, and guard themselves from using any arguments contained in this book to refute that which is taught in the Scripture, which is undoubtedly written by the Holy Spirit. But if he finds anything herein that serves for his instruction (as much of such is found), he shall not despise it, without paying heed to that which is mixed in here out of weakness; he shall do like a man who separates the honey for his use from the wax, and does not reject it because it is mixed with the wax.

<meta>This page transitions from the author’s justification for summarizing the history of the Maccabees into the narrative proper. It concludes the preface and begins Chapter 3, which details the attempted seizure of the Temple treasury by Heliodorus, an official of the Seleucid Empire.</meta>

Fol. 162.
# Of the Maccabees.

<margin>
Jason of Cyrene describes in his written History the pious and honorable virtues of Judas Maccabeus and his brothers, etc., from which history this book is taken as a short summary.
</margin>

**20** But the history of Judas the Maccabee and his brothers, and of the cleansing of the High Priest, and how the Altar was dedicated:

<margin>
k 1 Maccabees 1:11 / 6:17. 2 Maccabees 10:10.
</margin>

**21** And of the first reign of Antiochus the Noble <note>Known to history as Antiochus IV Epiphanes.</note>, <gloss>k</gloss> and his son Eupator;

<margin>
b This Antiochus was the eighth King of Syria in the 137th year, since the beginning of the Kingdom of Syria.
</margin>

**22** And of the signs from heaven, which were revealed to those who reasonably protected Judaism: that you, such a small group, plundered the whole land, and put a great multitude of the Heathen to flight, and pursued them.

**23** And further of the Temple, how it was rebuilt (as is already known everywhere) and the city regained its freedom: that all other laws were abolished, and only the Lord’s shall be kept, who is now well-disposed and merciful toward us.

**24** This and other things more, of which Jason made five books, we intend to condense here into a short summary.

**25** For we see that the number of stories is so mixed up with one another that it is difficult to properly grasp the histories while they lie in such a heap.

**26** Therefore we have wanted to make it so that people may read it gladly, and retain it more easily, and it may be useful to everyone.

**27** And it is true, we notice that it will be difficult for us to have taken on this labor: for it requires much work and great diligence.

**28** Just as it does not happen without labor for one who prepares a feast and wishes to please the guests: nevertheless, we do not want to look at that, and gladly take this trouble upon ourselves to serve others with it.

**29** In the histories themselves, we do not want to change anything, but let them remain as they were written before: except that we want to condense them more briefly.

**30** And just as a carpenter, when he builds a new house, thinks of nothing further than making it so that it is durable: but how it shall be painted and decorated, he lets another provide for that.

**31** So we also want to do, and will let the one who first wrote the histories provide for that—how he spoke all things and worked out all parts with diligence.

**32** But we do not want to do more than contain the sum in the shortest possible way.

**33** And we want now to take hold of the history, and have said this by way of introduction: so that the Preface does not become larger than the whole History.

### The 3rd Chapter.

*1. The piety and zeal of the high priest Onias, 4. Simon of the tribe of Benjamin, an enemy of Onias, 6. Heliodorus, wanting to carry out the King's commands, is severely punished by God, 32. Onias offers sacrifices and prays for Heliodorus, 35. Heliodorus offers to the Lord and travels back to the King and tells of the wonders of God performed in his person.*

**5** And since Onias was too powerful, he [Simon] went to Apollonius, son of Thraseas, the Governor in Coele-Syria <note>original: "neder Syria" (Lower Syria)</note> and Phoenicia.

**6** And told him how the treasury <note>original: "Gods kiste" (God's chest)</note> in Jerusalem was exceedingly rich in money, and had a great deal left over that was not needed for the sacrifice, and the King might well take it for himself.

**7** When Apollonius came to the King, he told him what Simon had said about the money. Then the King appointed Heliodorus his Chamberlain for this, and gave him the command that he should bring that same money to him.

**8** Heliodorus set out shortly after, and pretended he had to collect taxes in Coele-Syria and Phoenicia: but his intention was to carry out the King’s command.

**9** When he arrived in Jerusalem and the high priest had received him, he told him what his Lord had reported to him, and why he was there, and asked if it were so or not?

**10** Then the high priest answered him: "Part of it is placed with us for safekeeping <note>original: "tot trouwer hant gelept" (placed in a faithful hand/escrow)</note>, belonging to widows and orphans."

**11** "The other part belongs to Hyrcanus, son of Tobias, who was a distinguished man: and it was in no way as the traitor Simon had said: for it was no more than four hundred talents <term>centener</term> <note>A "centener" or hundredweight is used here to translate the biblical "talent," a massive unit of weight for precious metals.</note> of silver, and two hundred talents of gold."

**12** "So it would indeed be a great evil to take it away like that, and to deceive those who had trusted their property to the holy Temple, which is so highly honored and sanctified throughout the whole world."

**13** But Heliodorus stood by the command of the King: he must take it with him.

**14** And he came on a designated day into the Temple and wanted to inspect it: then a great sorrow arose throughout the whole city.

**16** But the high priest behaved so compassionately that no one could look at him without great pity: for one could see it in him, as he was so distraught in his countenance that he was in great agony.

1 [] The Samaritans had a temple in the mountains of Gerizim, located in Samaria. When they understood (as Josephus describes in Book 12, Chapter 7) the tyranny that Antiochus used against the Jews, they sent their ambassadors to Antiochus to make it known to him that they had no fellowship with the Jews, and that they willingly wished to submit to the King's ordinances. And regarding their Temple, it was not yet dedicated to any idol, and they were satisfied that it be understood as named for Jupiter of Crete <note>original: "Jupiter van Creten"</note>. When the King understood this, he commanded his servants that no harm should be done to these Samaritans, also consenting that their desire regarding the Temple should be granted.

1 Not long after, the King sent an old man from Antioch to force the Jews to fall away from the Law of their fathers and no longer keep God's Law.

2 And he was to defile the Temple in Jerusalem and call it the Church of Jupiter Olympus <note>original: "Jovis Olympii"</note>, and the Temple at Gerizim the Church of Jupiter, Protector of Strangers <note>original: "Jovis Xenij"</note>, since foreign people lived there.

15 But He prevents us, so that we do not make it too much, and so that He does not have to avenge Himself on us at the last.

16 Therefore He has never entirely taken His mercy from us; and even if He has already disciplined us with misfortune, He has nevertheless not entirely forsaken His people.

17 This I have wanted to say here as an admonition: now we will return to the history.

37 And they killed Timotheus, who had hidden himself in a pit, and Chereas his brother, and Apollophanes.

38 When they had accomplished all this, they praised the Lord with songs of praise, who had shown such great kindness to Israel and given them the victory.

9 Then they all praised the merciful God, and became so courageous that they were willing to strike down their enemies, even if they were the most wicked beasts or armored elephants <note>original: "peeren intieren" - a reference to war elephants equipped with towers</note> standing before them.

10 With such spirit, the entire army moved forward with their helper, whom the merciful God had sent to them from heaven.

11 And they attacked their enemies like lions, and slew eleven thousand of their infantry and sixteen hundred of their cavalry.

12 They drove all the others into flight, so that the majority who escaped were wounded; even Lysias himself fled shamefully and escaped.

13 However, Lysias was an intelligent man; as he considered the defeat he had suffered and saw that the Jewish people were invincible because the Almighty God stood by them:

14 He sent word to them and offered them peace on reasonable terms, promising them furthermore that he would persuade the King to become their good friend.

15 Maccabeus allowed himself to be pleased with this, for he saw that it was for the best; and the King consented to the covenant that Lysias had made with Maccabeus and the Jews.

16 And the letter which Lysias wrote to the Jews read as follows: "Lysias sends greetings to the Jews.

17 John and Absalom, your envoys, have delivered a letter and petitioned concerning the matters for which they were sent.

18 Whatever was necessary to bring before the King, I have done; and he has granted everything that is useful and possible.

19 If you now remain faithful and keep your word, I will also strive from now on to act for your best interest.

20 Concerning each specific point, your envoys and mine have instructions to inform you more fully."

<margin>4 The tyrant Antiochus was not yet dead in this year, or at least his son Antiochus Eupator had not yet ascended to the throne, for he only began to reign in the one hundred and forty-ninth year following.</margin>
<margin>5 This word is corrupted and placed in stead of the Greek word: *Dioscorinthion* <note>a month in the Seleucid calendar</note>; for the Greeks used the name of Jupiter <note>Zeus</note>. See 2 Maccabees 9:28.</margin>
21 "Farewell in God. Given in the one hundred and forty-eighth year, on the twenty-fourth day of the month Dioscori <note>likely the month Dystrus or Xanthicus</note>."

22 The King’s letter read as follows: "King Antiochus sends greetings to his brother Lysias:

23 Since our father has departed from us and has become a God <note>This refers to the deification of deceased Hellenistic kings</note>, nothing is dearer to us than that there should be peace in our kingdom, so that everyone may attend to his own affairs.

24 Now we hear that the Jews have not wished to consent to the changing of their religion to the heathen manner, but wish to remain in their own faith; they therefore pray that we would allow them to remain in it.

25 Since we now consider it good that this people also live in peace and be quiet, it is our intention that their temple be restored to them, and that they be allowed to live according to their own government and customs, as their forefathers held them.

26 Therefore, you should send some people to them and make peace with them, so that when they know our intention, they may be secure and go about their ways without any worry."

<column-break/>

27 The King’s letter to the Jews read as follows: "King Antiochus sends greetings to the Council and the community of the Jews.

28 If you are all doing well, that is our sincere hope; we also are doing well.

29 Menelaus has informed us how you desire to travel into our land and conduct your business among us.

30 Therefore, all Jews who travel between now and the thirtieth day of April shall have safe and secure passage.

31 They may observe their laws regarding food and other matters as before; also, no one shall suffer any harm for what has been done against us until now.

32 As a witness to this, we have chosen to send Menelaus to you, to give you further report of it.

33 Farewell in God. In the one hundred and forty-eighth year, on the fifteenth day of April."

34 The Romans also wrote to the Jews, as follows: "Quintus Memnius and Titus Manlius, envoys of the Romans, send their greetings to the Jews.

35 Everything that Lysias, the King’s uncle, has granted you, we also approve.

36 Since he now considers it good that certain points be brought before the King, deliberate among yourselves and send someone to us as soon as possible, so that we may reach an agreement with one another; for we are now traveling to Antioch.

37 Therefore, hurry and send some people here, so that we may know how you are minded.

38 Farewell in God."

Therefore, it is without doubt that human greed is the cause of such prayers for the dead; it is a harmful poison in the church of God because it causes the blood of Jesus Christ and the power of His suffering and death to be despised. 1 Tripolis is a city located on the Mediterranean Sea, Northwards from Tyre and Sidon / and this city is still very famous in this day / because of the multitude of worldly trades therein / for there are certainly a thousand who work in silk alone / there is also a fountain at Mount Lebanon a mile away from Tripoli / from which water flows into the center of the city.

1 **After** three years had passed, Judas and his men learned that Demetrius, the son of Seleucus <note>Demetrius I Soter, who escaped Rome to reclaim his father's throne.</note>, had arrived at Tripoli with a great army and many ships:

2 And he had taken the land, and had put Antiochus and his guardian Lysias to death.

3 And Alcimus, who had previously been High Priest, and during the time of the persecution had shamefully fallen away <note>He had adopted Greek customs and abandoned Jewish law.</note>: and now he thought that he could neither remain alive, nor return to the high priestly office,

4 He went to King Demetrius, in the one hundred and fifty-first year: and brought him a golden crown, and palm and olive branches, which belonged in the temple; and on the first day he held back, until he saw his time, which would be helpful to his madness.

5 When Demetrius had him called into the council and asked how it stood with the Jews, and what they intended to do.

6 Then he answered thus: The Jews who call themselves "the Pious" <note>original: "vromen" refers to the Hasideans, a strict religious sect.</note>, whose leader is Judas Maccabeus, are always stirring up war and uprising, and they do not allow the kingdom to have any peace.

7 They have also robbed me of my ancestral glory, namely, the Priesthood: therefore I have come here.

8 Firstly, for the King's benefit, and because I mean it faithfully: secondly, because I also gladly

<column-break/>

would provide counsel for my people: for with such disorder, our entire race shall perish.

9 Therefore, may the King look into the matter, and according to his highly-praised kindness, advise and help the land and our entire race in this matter.

10 For as long as Judas lives, it is not possible for there to be peace in the land.

11 When he had spoken such things, the others also grew angry against Judas, and incited Demetrius against him.

12 So he immediately called Nicanor, the captain of the elephant herd, to him, and appointed him as the commander against the Jews.

13 And he commanded him to kill Judas, and to scatter his followers, and to install Alcimus as the High Priest.

14 Then all the Heathens, whom Judas had driven out of the land, gathered themselves to Nicanor, and they hoped that the misfortune of the Jews would be their good fortune.

<margin>b 2 Maccabees 10:26. and 11:6.</margin>
15 When Judas and his men heard that Nicanor was marching against them, and that the Heathens were joining them in heaps from all sides, they sprinkled themselves with ashes, and called upon God, who had maintained His people since the beginning of the world, and had publicly helped His little flock.

16 When their commander gave the order, they set out and attacked the enemies near the village of Dessa.

17 And Simon, Judas's brother, attacked Nicanor, and Nicanor was nearly defeated, as the enemies seized him before he became aware of them.

18 When Nicanor heard that Judas had such brave men with him, who boldly risked life and limb for their fatherland, he feared him, and did not wish to hold a slaughter with him:

<margin>a To propose the conditions of peace.</margin>
19 But he sent Possidonius, Theodotus, and Mattathias to him, to make peace with him.

20 When they had consulted long over this, and their commander presented all the matters to the people, and they were in agreement, they consented to the treaty.

21 And they appointed a day when both of them should come together alone: When the day came, they set out a chair for each.

22 And Judas stationed some men in their armor not far away, lest the enemies should unexpectedly commit some evil act: and they spoke of their needs with one another.

23 And Nicanor remained for a time in Jerusalem, and undertook nothing against them, and he let his troops depart.

24 And he held Judas in high esteem before the people, and showed himself friendly toward him.

25 He also exhorted him to take a wife and father children: so Judas took a wife, and had good peace, and looked after his livelihood.

26 But when Alcimus saw that these two were at one with another and had made peace, he went again to Demetrius and accused Nicanor, saying that he had become unfaithful: for he had made Judas, the King's enemy, the successor to the kingdom.

<margin>v He speaks here of the feast that the Jews held in memory of Mordecai and Esther, who freed the Jews in Babylon from death. 6 The Holy Spirit speaking through the mouths of the Prophets and Apostles does not use this manner of apologizing for oneself, by which one can easily see that this book was not written by His inspiration.</margin>
38 So I will now conclude this book here, since Nicanor has perished and the Jews have won back the city.

39 And if I have made it pleasing, that I would like to see: but if it is too simple, then I have done as much as I was able.

40 For to drink only wine or only water at all times is not profitable, but sometimes to drink wine and sometimes water is pleasant: so it is also pleasant if one reads many different things. This be the end.

# THE THIRD BOOK
## OF THE MACCABEES.

---

-> To the Reader. <-

Since we find that in the French or Genevan copies, from which we have taken and translated these preceding annotations, this third book of the Maccabees is not printed, and the translator, out of his own boldness, did not want to undertake placing any foreign explanations—gathered from other authors—in the margins, seeing as such might be considered suspicious by many, it seemed good to us that we simply follow the Emden copy <note>The "Emden copy" refers to the Dutch Bible published in Emden, a major center for the Dutch Reformed movement in the 16th century.</note> here without changing or adding anything, just as it has been our intention to print and follow the same in the pursuit of the text throughout the entire Bible, and which we have now brought to an end by God's grace: praying that the favorable reader will take all of this in the best spirit.

---

### The First Chapter.

Herein is shown the horrible punishment for the blasphemous pride of Ptolemy. Also, the evil he later intended against the Jews, which God nevertheless graciously prevented and brought to a good end: making known to us thereby that the hearts of the King and of all men are in His hand.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'D' showing a seated royal figure, possibly a king, addressing individuals in a classical setting.</image-desc>

<margin>a Daniel 11:11.</margin>
1 **Philopator** <note>Ptolemy IV Philopator, King of Egypt (reigned 221–204 BC).</note> learned that some places he had held were taken from him by Antiochus.
2 So he summoned all his men of war, both on foot and on horse.
3 And he also took his sister Arsinoe with him, and set out for the region near Raphia <note>The Battle of Raphia (217 BC) was a major conflict between Ptolemy IV and Antiochus III the Great.</note>, where Antiochus' soldiers had their camp.
4 And one named Theodotus, seeking to accomplish the matter with cunning, took with him the most powerful of the soldiers who had been commanded to him by Ptolemy.
5 And he came to Ptolemy's tent at night to kill him, and thus bring an end to the war.
6 But Dositheus, the son of Drimylus <note>The OCR reads "Dytritli," likely a transcription error for the historical Drimylus.</note>, a born Jew,
7 who had nonetheless become an apostate <note>Someone who abandons their religious faith.</note> from the law and the ancestral institutions, had taken him away and placed an ignoble person in the tabernacle in his stead, who was then killed in his place.
8 And as a fierce slaughter took place, and Antiochus fought more strongly:
9 Arsinoe went everywhere among the army, with her hair loosened, and prayed mercifully with tears that they should boldly come to the aid of themselves, their children, and wives: and promised them, if they were victorious, to give two pounds of gold.
10 Thus it happened that the enemies were defeated, and many were taken prisoner.
11 Thereafter, having overcome the deceitful plot, he resolved to come to the surrounding cities and to strengthen them with his words.

<margin>b 3 Maccabees 3:16.</margin>
12 This he did, and presented the temples with gifts, and thus gave courage to his subjects.
13 But when the Jews had sent old men from their council to Philopator to greet him, present him with gifts, and wish him luck for the victory:
14 He conceived a greater desire to travel to them as soon as possible.

17 And when the Jews told him that such was not fitting, as it was not permitted even for the natives, nor even for the priests themselves, except for the one High Priest,

19 And even if that honor was denied to others, it ought not to be so for him.
20 And he also asked why no one present hindered him when he went into any other temples.
21 And when someone answered thoughtlessly that it was wrongly done:
22 He answered: "Even if it had not happened for some reason before, I shall go in there, whether they like it or not."
23 Then the priests, in all their robes, threw themselves down and prayed to the Great God that He would now come to their aid in this time of need and hinder the violence of those who wanted to do evil.
24 And as they thus filled the temple with howling and weeping,
25 others who were in the city became agitated and ran out, not knowing what had happened there.
26 Also the daughters, who were locked in their chambers, and the women in childbed, ran out, sprinkled their heads with dust and ashes, and filled the streets with weeping and lamentation.
27 And those who shortly before had adorned and prepared themselves to meet the King, forgot their becoming modesty and ran distractedly behind the city.

<margin>e 3 Maccabees 3:19.</margin>

### The 3rd Chapter.

1 **T**hen he became so very angry that he showed his wrath not only in Alexandria, but even more severely against those who lived elsewhere in the country: and commanded that they all be gathered immediately into one place and put to death with the most shameful punishments.

2 While this was happening, a very harmful rumor about the Jews spread everywhere, through which the people who were united in the Jews' destruction took cause to behave against them as if that people prevented the laws from being kept among them.

3 Nevertheless, the Jews remained immovable in their goodwill and loyalty toward the Kings: but because they served God and lived according to His laws, they kept themselves apart and drove certain things from them: for which reason they were regarded by some as enemies, although they were praiseworthy among all men for adorning their common life with good and righteous deeds.

4 So then the good fame of the Jews, which was spread everywhere, was now nowhere mentioned or regarded by the Heathens:

5 But that dispute, which the Jews had in their

<column-break/>

worship and in their customs, they [the Heathens] elevated and embittered with their tongues,

6 Saying that the Jews were friends neither of the Kings nor of the authorities, but were enemies, and stood greatly against the common welfare: thus they accused them heavily.

7 But there were Greeks in the city to whom no wrong had been done; seeing that an unforeseen riot and thoughtless assault was happening against those people, they were troubled because they could not give them any help.

8 For it was an entirely tyrannical business:

9 So they comforted them, having great displeasure [at the events], and hoped for a change in such things:

10 Saying that such reckless and frivolous conduct could not stand.

11 Some neighbors and friends, and those who were their companions in trade, secretly took some of them in, and promised to give help and to protect them with all diligence.

### The 4th Chapter.

1 And in whatever places this mandate was brought, there the Pagans held a common feast, with joy and rejoicing, as the hatred that had long been hardened in their hearts was now openly revealed.
2 But the Jews were in very bitter sorrow, and gave forth a very piteous sound with weeping; their hearts were everywhere full of sighing, sensing that unforeseen and sudden destruction which came upon them through the King’s sentence.
3 There was no land, no city, nor inhabited place, nor any road, that was not filled with their sighing and weeping.
4 For they were sent away with so bitter a sentence from all the Governors, that even some of their enemies, seeing the unusual punishment and the common misery before their eyes, and considering the uncertain changes of life, lamented their very miserable deportation.

<column-break/>

5 For there was led a multitude of old men, covered with gray hair.
6 Whose legs, which were slow and bent with age, were mistreated by the violent driving with heavy threats to move quickly upon the road.
7 And the daughters who had recently entered into the state of marriage received sorrow instead of joy.
8 And they were led with open heads, their hair that had been washed with fragrant ointment now being smothered with ashes:
9 And instead of merry wedding songs, they began a lamentation together:
10 As those who were torn by the Pagans' mockery and bound, they were openly and with violence dragged into the ship.
11 Likewise their husbands, having nooses <note>original: "stroppē"</note> around their necks instead of crowns, spent the remaining days of their wedding in sorrow during their youthful prime, instead of the feast and rest of the young, now seeing death before their eyes.
12 They were led away like beasts, pulled with iron bands.
13 Some were fastened by the neck to the sides of the ships, some were made fast by the legs with firm bonds in the bottom of the ship, and a thick hatch was closed over their heads, so that their eyes were entirely blinded, and they were treated like traitors throughout the entire voyage.
14 When they had been brought by ship according to the King's command, the King ordered that they should be placed in tents on that vast race-field <note>The Hippodrome of Alexandria, a large stadium used for chariot racing.</note> that is before the city, as a very convenient place for all who came to the city and rode out of the city to see the example of the punishment:
15 And he did not deign to let them enjoy the fellowship of his people, nor the enclosure of the city walls.
16 When this had happened, and the King heard that some Jews from the city had secretly come out to their people and had often lamented the grisly misery of their brothers:
17 He became very angry, and commanded that these also should be treated cautiously like the others, and the punishment upon them should in no way be diminished.
18 He also commanded that the entire people should be registered by their names.
19 For he no longer wished to plague them with the laborious servitude ordained a short time before:
20 But with selected punishment, to destroy them all in one day.
21 So they were then registered with bitter diligence, and though they sat at it from the rising of the sun until the setting of the sun for forty days, the registration was still not completed.
<margin>a 3 Maccabees 6:37.</margin>

23 And with his blasphemous mouth, praising the mute and helpless images, and speaking against the most high God that which was not becoming.

### The 5th Chapter.

<margin>a 1 Maccabees 6:34.</margin>
1 Then the King, being seized with heavy anger and irreconcilable fury, called Hermon, the chief over the care of the elephants, to him, and commanded that on the following day he should give all the elephants (which were five hundred in number) much incense to eat, with an abundance of pure wine to drink, so that, being wild and fierce from that excessive drink, they might be brought forth to the killing of the Jews.

2 And when he had given this command, he called together the chief of his friends and his soldiers, and being hostiley minded toward the Jews, he gave himself over to feasting.

3 Hermon, the master of the elephants, fulfilled that command well.

4 And the servants went out toward evening and bound the hands of the miserable ones, and further attended to everything that was to be done to them:

5 Thinking that those people must all be destroyed together in the morning.

6 But the Jews, who, being bound everywhere with heavy chains, appeared to the heathens to be deprived of all help and protection,

7 All called without ceasing and with tears upon the almighty Lord, their merciful God and Father, who is above all power.

8 Praying that he would turn away the godless counsel against them and deliver them from that great destruction, which was unhindered before their eyes.

<margin>b Sirach 21:6.</margin>
9 And their constant prayer ascended into Heaven.

10 But Hermon, who had now filled the cruel elephants with an abundance of wine and sated them with incense, came in the morning to the King’s court to make the matter known to the King.

<margin>c 1 Samuel 26:7.</margin>
11 But He who from the beginning of the world ordains day and night for that fair creation, and gives to each one as He wills, sent a sleep upon the King; and the working of the Lord made him sleep so sweetly and deeply that his evil intent failed him, and his irreconcilable sentence was greatly delayed.

12 When the Jews now saw that the hour of pillage had passed, they praised their holy and personal God,

<column-break/>

and prayed again that He would show the power of His mighty hand to the heathens.

13 When it was now about half past nine <note>original: "half ure thiene"—literally "half hour to ten," a traditional way of saying 9:30</note>, and the Watchmaster saw that the guests were there, he went to the King and could hardly wake him, and announced that the time for the meal was now passing while he spoke with him.

14 Whereupon the King, being reminded, came forth and had those who had come for the meal take their seats.

15 And when they were seated, he exhorted them to make good cheer and, giving themselves over to joy, to honor the present time of the meal.

16 But when the talk grew long, the King called Hermon to him and asked him bitterly with threats why the Jews were still left alive that day?

17 And when Hermon complained to him that he had fulfilled the King’s command the previous night, and his friends testified to the same, he answered again like Phalaris <note>Phalaris was a Greek tyrant of Sicily famous for his extreme cruelty, specifically for executing enemies inside a bronze bull.</note>.

18 They may thank today's sleep for that: but prepare the elephants in the same manner without delay against tomorrow, for the destruction of the wicked Jews.

19 When all who were present, being blinded, had praised this command of the King, each went to his own house.

<margin>d Micah 2:1.</margin>

21 Then, as soon as the cock first crowed in the morning, Hermon began to bring the armed beasts into the great place:

22 And the people from the entire city gathered for that miserable spectacle, eagerly awaiting the light of day.

23 But the Jews were sighing all that time, and with prayers and mournful singing and lifting of hands toward Heaven, they called upon the supreme God, that He would again quickly help them.

24 Before the sun was fully up, while the King was receiving his friends, Hermon stood and called to the Lord <note>Here referring to the King as "Lord" in the feudal sense.</note>, signifying that the King’s will was prepared.

25 When the King heard this, he was astonished by that fearful outing, as one who had forgotten everything, and asked what was happening and why he did such things so earnestly?

<meta>This page concludes the Third Book of Maccabees. It follows the dramatic scene where King Ptolemy IV Philopator, witnessing divine intervention, suddenly reverses his decree to execute the Jewish population of Egypt. The King now issues a royal edict protecting the Jews and allowing them to punish those among their own people who abandoned their faith under pressure.</meta>

# The Third Book of the Maccabees.

40 The King praised them/ and sent to the governors of every city this following letter/ in which the great change of his heart is reflected.

## Chapter 7.

1 King Ptolemy Philopator/ wishes the Governors throughout Egypt/ and the officers of the government/ salvation and welfare: for it goes well with us and our children.
2 Since the great God/ has given prosperity to our affairs according to our will/
3 Some friends <note>In the Hellenistic court, "Friends" was a formal title for the King's inner circle of advisors.</note> have frequently and sternly approached us/ and led us to believe/ that we should gather the Jews who are in our kingdom into one place/ and kill them as enemies with unusual punishment.
4 Saying/ that because of the hatred/ which the Jews have against all Heathens/ our kingdom would never have peace/ until that was done.
5 And when they had brought them here bound/ with great torment/ like slaves/ even like traitors/ they sought to kill them without any investigation or hearing of their cause/ using more than Scythian <note>The Scythians were an ancient nomadic people often cited by Greeks and Romans as the ultimate example of barbaric cruelty.</note> cruelty.
6 And when we bitterly scolded them for this/ according to the justice we practice toward all men/ we have through our mercy barely allowed the Jews to escape with their lives.
7 But we have certainly found/ that the Heavenly God protects the Jews/ and like a father to his children/ has helped them in all things.
8 Also considering the steadfast and well-meaning friendship/ that they show us/ (as they also did in former times to our ancestors)/ we rightly declare them free from all accusation whatever it may be: and command every person/ that they be allowed to return to their own/ in whatever place it may be/ so that absolutely no one hinders them/ nor reproaches them for anything/ that they have unjustly suffered.
<margin>a Jeremiah 30:16. Zechariah 2:5.</margin>
9 For know/ that if we begin anything evil against them/ or grieve them in any way/ not a man/ but the supreme God and Ruler of all power/ will visibly/ in all things/ always and without hindrance avenge them. Fare well.
<margin>b 3 Maccabees 2:30.</margin>
10 When they had received this letter/ they did not depart immediately/ but also requested of the King/ that the Jews who had voluntarily abandoned the holy God and his law/ might be punished by them/ according to their merit:
11 Because those/ who for the sake of the belly/ <note>This refers to those who prioritized physical survival or material comfort over religious law.</note>

<column-break/>

had transgressed the commandments of God/ would never be faithful to the King.
12 Since the King judged/ that it was true/ just as they said/ he praised them/ and gave them power/ to kill those who had abandoned the law of God/ in all places of his kingdom/ without any mediation of Royal power/ or further investigation.
13 Then they thanked the King/ (as was fitting)/ and their Priests and the whole multitude/ cried out *Alleluia* <note>original: "Alleluja" - a Hebrew expression of praise meaning "Praise the Lord."</note>/ and went away with joy.
14 And so on the way/ they punished the transgressors of their people/ and killed them as an example/ indeed on that day they killed more than three hundred/ and made joy and gladness/ killing the godless.
15 But those who had clung to God even unto death/ went out of the city/ crowned with all kinds of very fragrant flowers/ with joy and shouting/ with hymns and very sweet singing/ having regained the perfect fruit of their deliverance.
16 And when they had come to the city of Ptolemais/ named for the nature of the place/ *Rhodophoros*/ (that is/ **Rose-bearing**/)/ where they were expected by the ships/ they held a feast there for seven days by common counsel/ while the King kindly provided all necessities for the journey for every person/ until they reached home.
17 Thus they departed safely/ with appropriate rejoicing/ and thought it good/ to also keep those joyful days there as a memorial of their pilgrimage.
18 And when they had erected a memorial column there/ they departed by land and water safely/ free/ and joyful.
19 And by the King's command/ every person was restored unharmed/ back to his house/
20 Having regained greater power than before/ against their enemies/ with honor and terrifying presence:
21 And they were not at all/ robbed of their property by anyone:
22 For they regained all their goods according to the previous inventory/ so that all those/ who had anything of theirs/ returned it to them with great fear:
23 Since the supreme God with great deeds/ accomplished their salvation.
24 The savior of Israel/ is to be praised for eternity/ Amen.
